#### Common Misconception

The most important thing to understand about any between-group gap is that _a difference in group averages is not a fact about group members._ The statement "median white wealth is about six times median Black wealth" is a statement about two _medians_ , two typical points in two wide distributions. It is emphatically _not_ a statement that white individuals have six times the wealth of Black individuals, and it is consistent with enormous overlap between the two distributions: millions of Black families with more wealth than millions of white families, vast ranges within each group, and individual lives that the group average cannot predict. The _between-group_ gap (the difference in averages) and the _within-group_ variance (the spread inside each group) are different quantities, and the within-group variance is, for almost every group on almost every measure, _much larger_ than the between-group gap. To read a group average as a claim about any individual, or to treat a group as internally uniform, is a basic statistical error and also a moral one, because it erases the individual person into a category. Every group gap in this chapter is a fact about distributions, and a person is never a distribution. Hold this guard especially hard here, because nowhere is the slide from "group difference" to "claim about individuals" more tempting or more damaging.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
### 17.2 The causes: running the full decomposition

Now we cross, with a clear marker, from the settled measurement (the gap exists and is roughly this large) into the contested terrain of _why_. The existence is settled; the causes run the full Chapter 15 decomposition, with the residual's clusters held at equal standing and no verdict smuggled in. Let us lay out the major families of explanation, each at its strongest, none crowned.

The **historical-legacy** account, stated at full strength: wealth is precisely the thing that accumulates and inherits across generations (Chapter 8), so a gap that opened in the past, through historical exclusion from the very mechanisms of wealth-building, will persist into the present by the ordinary compounding logic of Chapter 8 even if all present-day treatment were identical, because the descendants of those who could not accumulate start with less to inherit, less to pass on, less cushion to convert risk into opportunity. On this account, much of the wealth gap is the long shadow of history operating through the entirely ordinary machinery of inheritance. Notably, it does not depend on contested claims about the present; it follows from the inheritance mechanics we already established and the historical fact of past exclusion. This is a genuine logical feature of the legacy account, not a mark of superiority, and the other three accounts have their own evidentiary footing in turn: the structural account can point to direct, matched-application measurement of present-day treatment, the measurable-factors account to observable mediating variables that can be tallied, and the cultural account, read with the two-way guard of Chapter 14, to documented patterns of practice. Each of the four rests on a different kind of evidence, and which set of premises is "firmest" is not a ranking this chapter makes.

The **structural-and-treatment** account, at full strength: present-day mechanisms, not only past ones, continue to shape the gap, through the channels of Part 3 operating unequally, unequal access to the neighborhoods and schools that build advantage, to the networks that open opportunities, to credit and homeownership (the largest wealth-builder for most families), plus discrimination that, as we saw, is real and measured in specific settings. On this account, the gap is sustained not only by history's shadow but by present arrangements that distribute wealth-building opportunities unequally.

The **differences-in-measurable-factors** account, at full strength: part of the gap is associated with measurable differences that themselves bear on wealth accumulation, differences in income (which feeds saving), in age structure, in family structure, in education, in inheritance received, in patterns of saving and asset-holding. To the extent these factors differ across groups, they account for part of the wealth gap in the decomposition sense, though, exactly as in Chapter 16, "accounted for by" does not mean "innocent," because those factors themselves have causes (including the historical and structural ones above) and their own freedom is contested.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
The **cultural** account, at full strength and with the Chapter 14 care: there may be group differences in patterns of saving, investing, asset preference, or financial practice that contribute at the margin, understood, in the disciplined Lewis-style sense, as potentially _adaptive responses_ to historical and structural conditions rather than as free-floating "values," and held with the same protection from caricature in both directions that we gave the culture-of-poverty debate. This account must be neither inflated into "the gap is their own fault" nor reflexively declared unspeakable; like the other three, it is one possible contributing factor, structurally rooted, of contested weight.


#### Definition: Settled Measurement vs. Contested Cause

A **settled measurement** is an IS so robustly established that manufacturing a debate over its _existence_ is itself a balance failure (false balance): it must be stated plainly. A **contested cause** is a WHY, an account of _why_ the settled measurement exists, where genuine debate among serious people is real and the steelman duty applies. The discipline is to _never confuse them_ : do not fake a debate over the settled measurement, and do not present any contested cause as if it shared the measurement's settledness. The wealth gap's _size_ is a settled measurement; its _causes_ are contested; and a contested _normative verdict_ about whether it is unjust is a third thing again, never settled.

In plain language: that the gap exists is not up for debate; why it exists is genuinely up for debate; whether it is unjust is a separate value question. Three registers, one gap, kept rigorously apart, the is/why/ought discipline of Chapter 2 in its most charged application. Notice the asymmetry from the pay-gap chapter: there, even the gross figure invited "it's a myth" denials we had to rebut; here, the measurement is settled enough that the live danger flips to false balance, and the steelman duty lives entirely on the _causal_ side, where it belongs. Learning to feel which danger is live, denial of a real measurement, or fake debate over a settled one, is the judgment this chapter trains.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
### 17.3 Holding the causal decomposition honest

The causes above are not rivals to be ranked into a winner; all four mechanisms operate, their relative weights are genuinely contested, and this chapter does not rank them. To do otherwise would be to commit the very error Chapter 15 named: apportionment-as-argument, the move that pre-weights some accounts above others and hands the reader a verdict dressed as a description. Saying "this account carries substantial support and that one is merely debated" treats a contested apportionment as if it were a settled measurement, which is exactly what we are forbidden to do here, where the _size_ of the gap is settled but the _weights of its causes_ are not. So we state the weights as contested, full stop, and leave the weighing to the reader. But honesty here requires more than listing the accounts and declining to rank them; it requires applying the residual discipline at maximum pressure, because this is exactly where apportionment-as-argument creeps in.

First, the discrimination distinction, once more, because it is indispensable: discrimination by race in housing, lending, hiring, and evaluation is _real and measured in specific settings_ , this is a settled IS, established by careful studies including matched-application designs. _And_ the _share_ of the aggregate wealth gap attributable to present-day discrimination is _not_ directly measured; it is a contested interpretation, because the aggregate gap mixes present discrimination with history's compounding shadow and with the measurable factors, and no study cleanly apportions the whole. Both halves, again: discrimination is real and measured (do not deny it), and its precise share of this gap is contested (do not assume it). The same two-part discipline as the pay gap.

Second, the "explained" trap, race edition. When a decomposition finds that part of the wealth gap is "accounted for" by, say, income differences, the careless analyst on one side concludes "so it's not about race, it's about income." This commits Chapter 15's trap two: it forgets to ask _why_ the groups differ in income, which itself may run through the historical and structural channels, so the income difference may be race operating _through_ a measured factor, not instead of it. The careless analyst on the other side commits trap one, treating the entire unexplained residual as present-day discrimination, when it also contains history's shadow and unmeasured factors. Both inflate; the discipline holds the explained portion's own causes open and the residual's clusters at equal standing.

Third, and crucial for keeping the IS register clean, none of this causal contestation reaches back to unsettle the _measurement_. That the causes are debated does not make the gap's existence debatable. A common and corrosive move is to use genuine causal uncertainty ("we can't be sure how much is discrimination versus history versus income") to cast doubt on the gap itself ("so maybe it's overstated"). No. The size is settled; the causal uncertainty lives entirely downstream of it. Keeping the settled measurement firmly stated even while the causes are fought over is the precise discipline this chapter exists to teach.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
### 17.4 The comparative eye and the gentle caution

Two final disciplines, the first to widen the view and the second to keep it humane.

The comparative eye, applied here, cuts against treating any one society's racial arrangement as the universal shape of group inequality. Between-group inequality takes profoundly different forms across societies: which groups are advantaged or disadvantaged, the histories that produced the gaps, the categories themselves (what counts as a "group" is socially and historically specific and varies enormously across societies), and the size and trend of the gaps all differ. A reader formed entirely on one country's racial story can mistake its particular categories and history for the universal template, which is exactly the error Chapter 1 warned against. Group gaps are real in many societies; their _shape_ is particular to each, and the honest analyst says which society, which groups, which history, which as-of, every time, and does not export one nation's template onto another or treat any society (including the reader's own, and including others one might be tempted to caricature) as the human default.

The gentle caution returns us to the within-group guard, now with its full human weight. Every account in this chapter is about _distributions_ , group averages and their spreads, and a person is never a distribution. The Black family with substantial wealth and the white family with none are not statistical errors; they are among the millions who populate the overlap between the distributions, and their lives are not predicted by the group average. To keep faith with them, we must say clearly what the group statistics do and do not claim: they describe real differences in averages, produced by real and contested causes, _and_ they say nothing about any individual, who remains an agent whose life the category cannot foretell. The gap is real and worth understanding; the individual is real and not reducible to the gap. Holding both is the difference between sociology and stereotype, and on this subject the difference is everything.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
### 17.5 What Part 6 has built

Part 6 took us across the gaps between groups, the terrain where opposing camps most often wield the same numbers as weapons, and it did so with method rather than reflex. Chapter 15 built the instrument: the decomposition of a gross gap into an explained portion and a residual, the two traps of inflating either, the residual's two clusters held at equal standing, and the distinction between discrimination's _measured existence_ and its _contested share_. Chapter 16 applied it to the pay gap, modeling all five steps and the crossing into the normative. This chapter added the final discipline, the difference between a _settled measurement_ (stated plainly, never faked into a debate) and a _contested cause_ (run through the full decomposition), and the dangers specific to each, false balance for the former, smuggled verdicts for the latter, plus the comparative eye and the within-group guard that group gaps especially demand.

The tools are now complete. We have learned to measure inequality (Part 0), to define class (Part 1), to see how position shapes lives (Part 2) and passes down (Part 3) and how much it passes down (Part 4), to understand poverty (Part 5), and to read group gaps without joining a tribe (Part 6). Through all of it, one register has been deliberately held in reserve: the OUGHT. We have separated it, marked it, and refused it, again and again, promising that the strongest cases on every side would come in Part 7. That promise now comes due. Part 7 turns from _what is_ and _why_ to the question the whole book has been circling and declining to answer: _is inequality just?_ It is the contested heart, and we enter it the way we have done everything, by giving every serious position its strongest form and crowning none, beginning with the oldest and most provocative claim of all: that a society _needs_ its inequality, that stratification is not a flaw but a function.


### 17.6 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Explain the difference between a "settled measurement" and a "contested cause," using the racial wealth gap, and state the specific failure that threatens each.

Hint

Which is the _existence and size_ of the gap, and which is _why_ it exists? What is the danger of faking a debate, and the danger of smuggling a verdict?

**Answer:** A _settled measurement_ is an IS so robustly established that debating its _existence_ is itself a balance failure. The racial wealth gap's _size_ , the typical white family holding roughly six times the wealth of the typical Black family and roughly four to five times the typical Hispanic family (US, recent Federal Reserve data), is a settled measurement: found across sources and decades, not in dispute. A _contested cause_ is a WHY, an account of _why_ the gap exists (historical legacy, present structural mechanisms, differences in measurable factors, cultural factors), where genuine debate among serious people is real and the steelman duty applies. The failure threatening the settled measurement is _false balance_ , faking a debate over whether the gap exists ("some studies suggest possible disparities"), which is cowardice, not even-handedness. The failure threatening the contested cause is _smuggling a verdict_ , presenting one causal story as if it shared the measurement's settledness, or letting the plainly-stated gap imply its own explanation. The discipline is to never confuse them: state the measurement plainly, run the causes through the full contested decomposition.

**Q2.** Why does the chapter insist that "a difference in group averages is not a fact about group members," and why is the within-group variance usually larger than the between-group gap?

Hint

The gap compares two _medians_ (or means) of two wide distributions. What does that allow about overlap between the distributions and about any individual?

**Answer:** A group gap (like "median white wealth is about six times median Black wealth") compares two _typical points_ in two _wide distributions_ ; it is not a claim that any white individual has six times any Black individual's wealth. It is fully consistent with enormous _overlap_ between the distributions, millions of Black families with more wealth than millions of white families, and vast ranges within each group, so it cannot predict any individual's wealth. The within-group variance (the spread inside each group) is usually _much larger_ than the between-group gap because each group spans nearly the whole range from very poor to very rich, while the gap is only a difference between the two groups' middles; the internal spread dwarfs the difference between the averages. Reading a group average as a fact about individuals, or treating a group as internally uniform, is both a statistical error (confusing a distribution with a point) and a moral one (erasing the individual into a category). The chapter stresses this guard hardest here because the slide from "group difference" to "claim about individuals" is most tempting and most damaging on race.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A decomposition finds that part of the racial wealth gap is "accounted for" by differences in income between groups. One commentator says "so it's about income, not race." Another says "the entire unexplained remainder is present-day discrimination." Diagnose both errors using Chapter 15's two traps, and give the disciplined statement.

Hint

For the first: _why_ do the groups differ in income, could race operate _through_ income? For the second: what besides present discrimination lives in the residual (recall the historical-legacy account)?

**Answer:** The first commentator commits _trap two_ (inflating the explained portion into innocence): saying "it's about income, not race" forgets to ask _why_ the groups differ in income, which itself may run through the historical and structural channels, so the income difference may be _race operating through_ a measured factor, not instead of it. "Accounted for by income" does not mean "not about race." The second commentator commits _trap one_ (inflating the residual into discrimination): treating the entire unexplained remainder as present-day discrimination ignores that the residual also contains _history's compounding shadow_ (the historical-legacy account, which needs no present discrimination to persist) and _unmeasured factors_ ; the residual is a measure of ignorance, not a measure of present discrimination. The disciplined statement: part of the gap is associated with income differences _whose own causes may include the historical and structural channels_ (so "explained" is not "innocent"), and the residual contains a discrimination cluster (real, measured in specific settings, of contested share) _and_ the legacy of past exclusion compounding through inheritance _and_ unmeasured factors, held at equal standing, with the decomposition adjudicating none of them.

**Q2.** For _each_ of the four accounts of the wealth gap (historical-legacy, structural-and-treatment, differences-in-measurable-factors, cultural), state in one sentence what premises it rests on and what it cannot by itself measure. Then explain why stating these features for one account, but not the others, would itself be a balance failure.

Hint

Each account rests on some premises (some about the past, some about the present) and none, on its own, fixes its _share_ of the aggregate gap. Recall §17.3: the _weights_ of the causes are contested, full stop.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src: **Answer:** _Historical-legacy_ : rests on the inheritance mechanics of Chapter 8 plus the historical fact of past exclusion (premises not seriously disputed, and notably not about the present); it cannot by itself measure how much of the present gap is its doing. _Structural-and-treatment_ : rests on present-day mechanisms (unequal access to neighborhoods, schools, networks, credit, homeownership) plus discrimination that is real and measured in specific settings; it cannot by itself measure its _share_ of the aggregate gap, which mixes with history and measured factors. _Differences-in-measurable-factors_ : rests on observable group differences (income, age, family, education) that bear on accumulation; it cannot tell us _why_ those factors differ, so "accounted for" is not "innocent." _Cultural_ : rests on possible group differences in saving or asset practice, held in the disciplined Lewis-style as adaptive responses to structure; it cannot by itself measure its weight and is most prone to caricature in both directions. Stating these features for one account alone would be a balance failure of the apportionment-as-argument kind (§17.3): giving one account more air-time, more vividness, or its own dedicated treatment hands the reader a ranking dressed as a description, when the _weights of the causes are contested, full stop_. The honest move is to hold all four at equal standing and let the reader weigh.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** This chapter says the existence of a gap can be _settled_ while its causes are _contested_ and its justice is a _third, open question_. Take the racial wealth gap and trace how three people could agree completely that the gap exists and is large, agree substantially on its causes, and _still_ disagree about whether it is unjust and what (if anything) should be done. What does this show about the relationship between history, cause, and verdict?

**Discussion:** This question integrates the chapter's three-register discipline at its most charged, and it shows, once more, that even agreement on the facts and the causes does not produce agreement on the verdict, because the verdict rests on value premises the facts cannot supply.

Grant all three people the settled measurement (the gap is real and large) and even substantial agreement on causes (say, they agree on roughly the same mix of historical, structural, measurable-factor, and cultural contributions, however they apportion the weights). They can still diverge sharply on justice and response.

Person One holds that justice is fundamentally _backward-looking_ and concerned with rectification: if the present gap is largely the compounded result of past injustice (exclusion that was wrong when it happened), then the present distribution inherits that wrongness, and a society has an obligation to address it precisely _because_ of how it came about. For this person, the causal story (history's shadow) does heavy normative work: the gap is unjust because its lineage is unjust, and something is owed.

Person Two holds that justice is fundamentally _forward-looking_ and concerned with present and future treatment, not with the lineage of current holdings. This person can fully agree that past exclusion was wrong and _still_ hold that what justice requires now is that present arrangements treat everyone fairly going forward, not that present holdings be rearranged according to their history. For this person, the same causal story (history's shadow) does _not_ establish a present obligation to close the gap, because they locate justice in the fairness of present rules, not in the ancestry of present wealth. Note that Persons One and Two can agree on every fact and every cause and still disagree, because they hold different _theories of what justice is about_ (rectification versus present fairness), which is a value question, not a factual one, and which we will meet head-on in Chapter 20 as the clash between historical and present-time-slice principles of justice.

Person Three holds that justice is about _present outcomes and need_ regardless of history or causal lineage: for this person, what matters is not how the gap arose but whether anyone is presently deprived, so they might support addressing deprivation wherever it falls (across all groups) while being indifferent to the _racial_ composition of the gap as such, caring about the bottom of every group rather than the difference between group averages. This person agrees on facts and causes too, and still reaches a different practical conclusion, because their value premise locates justice in outcomes, not in groups or in history.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src: What this shows is the book's deepest structure, here at maximum charge: _history_ (what happened), _cause_ (why the present gap exists), and _verdict_ (whether it is unjust and what to do) are three distinct things, and the move from the first two to the third _always_ requires a value premise, specifically, a theory of what justice is fundamentally about (rectification of past wrongs, fairness of present rules, or decency of present outcomes), and reasonable people hold different such theories. This is why establishing the cause, even establishing that the gap descends from acknowledged historical injustice, does not by itself settle the verdict: the backward-looking, forward-looking, and outcome-focused theories of justice are genuinely contested, and which you hold determines what the agreed facts and causes _mean_ for what should be done. The chapter's discipline, state the measurement, debate the causes, and keep the verdict separate and open, is not evasion; it is the recognition that the verdict turns on a contested theory of justice that the next Part will lay out in full, with every position given its strongest form and none crowned. The facts and causes are the input to that argument. They are not the argument, and they do not end it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 17: Race, Origin, and the Wealth Gap
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

This chapter taught the discipline of distinguishing a **settled measurement** from a **contested cause** , using gaps by race and origin. The racial wealth gap's _size_ is a settled measurement, stated plainly: in the US, the typical white family holds roughly six times the wealth of the typical Black family and roughly four to five times the typical Hispanic family (recent Federal Reserve data), with the wealth gap far larger than the income gap because wealth compounds and inherits (Chapter 2). With a settled measurement, the live danger flips from denial to _false balance_ : we must state it plainly and refuse to fake a debate over its existence, while installing the **within-group variance guard** , a group-average difference is _not_ a fact about group members, the distributions overlap enormously, and the within-group spread dwarfs the between-group gap, so a person is never a distribution.

We then ran the _causes_ through the full contested decomposition, each account at full strength, none crowned: the **historical-legacy** account (a past gap compounding through ordinary inheritance, persisting without requiring present discrimination), the **structural-and-treatment** account (present mechanisms and measured discrimination distributing wealth-building unequally), the **differences-in-measurable-factors** account (income, age, family, education, where "accounted for" is not "innocent"), and the **cultural** account (held in the disciplined Lewis-style, structurally-rooted, protected from caricature in both directions). We applied the residual discipline at maximum pressure: discrimination is _real and measured in specific settings_ while its _share of the aggregate gap is contested_ ; the "explained" trap and the residual-inflation trap were diagnosed in their race editions; and crucially, causal contestation does _not_ reach back to unsettle the measurement.

Two final disciplines: the _comparative eye_ (between-group inequality takes different forms across societies, no society's racial arrangement is the universal template, always name which society, groups, history, and as-of) and the _humane within-group caution_ (the statistics describe real average differences from contested causes _and_ say nothing about any individual agent). The Think Deeper showed that three people can agree on the settled measurement and substantially on causes and _still_ disagree on the verdict, because the move from history and cause to verdict requires a contested _theory of justice_ (rectification, present fairness, or outcome/need), which Part 7 will lay out.

The tools are now complete. Part 7 turns at last to the OUGHT held in reserve through the whole book: _is inequality just?_ It begins with the most provocative claim of all, that a society _needs_ its inequality, that stratification is a function, not a flaw.

* * *

---

For seventeen chapters we have held one question in reserve. We have measured inequality, defined it, traced how it shapes lives and passes down, counted the poor, and read the gaps between groups, and at every turn, when the question of _fairness_ pressed in, we set it aside with a promise: not yet, the verdict comes in Part 7. That promise now comes due. We turn, at last, from _what is_ and _why_ to the question the whole book has been circling: _is inequality just?_ And we enter it the way we have done everything else, by giving each serious position its strongest form and crowning none, because on this question above all, a book that delivered a verdict would be worthless to the half of its readers who disagreed.

We begin with the most provocative possible answer, one that scandalizes many people on first hearing and that deserves, for exactly that reason, to be stated at full strength before it is judged. It is the claim that a society does not merely _have_ inequality but in some sense _needs_ it, that stratification is not a flaw in the social machine but a working part of it. This is the functionalist theory of stratification, and it has a classic statement, a classic critique, and a rival tradition that rejects its entire framing. Working through all three is the perfect opening to Part 7, because it forces us, immediately, to separate a question about _function_ (does inequality do useful work?) from a question about _justice_ (is it therefore fair?), and to see that even a convincing answer to the first would not settle the second.


### 18.1 The functionalist case, stated at full strength

The argument is associated with a famous statement by the sociologists Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore (1945), and it runs as follows. Begin with a problem every society must solve: it has many positions to fill, and they are not equally important or equally easy to fill. Some positions are more functionally important than others (the society depends more on their being done, and done well), and some require scarce talent, long training, or the bearing of heavy burdens. A society must somehow ensure that its most important and most demanding positions are actually filled, and filled by capable people who undertake the necessary training and discharge the duties conscientiously.

How does a society accomplish this? The Davis-Moore answer: by attaching _unequal rewards_ to positions, more income, prestige, and privilege to the positions that are both more important and harder to fill. These differential rewards function as incentives. They motivate the talented to undergo the long and costly training that demanding positions require, and to take on the burdens and responsibilities those positions carry, rather than choosing easier paths. On this account, stratification, the unequal distribution of rewards across positions, is a _mechanism_ by which a society induces the right people to do the most important and most difficult work. Remove the unequal rewards, and you remove the incentive; remove the incentive, and you risk the most demanding positions going unfilled or filled by the unwilling and unprepared.

#### Definition: The Davis-Moore Thesis (functionalist theory of stratification)

The **Davis-Moore thesis** holds that social stratification is _functionally necessary_ : because a society must fill positions that differ in functional importance and in the talent or training they require, it must attach _unequal rewards_ (income, prestige, privilege) to those positions in order to motivate capable people to seek the more important and more demanding ones and to bear the costs of preparing for them. On this view, unequal rewards are an incentive mechanism that helps ensure vital work gets done, so some degree of inequality is a working feature of any complex society, not merely an accident or an injustice.

In plain language: the functionalist says inequality is, at least in part, the price a society pays to get its hardest and most important jobs done well. State the case at its most compelling, because it is more compelling than its detractors often admit. It explains something real, that across a vast range of societies, including ones that explicitly tried to abolish material inequality, demanding and important roles have tended to carry greater rewards, which suggests the incentive logic is tapping something genuine about how people respond to reward. It connects directly to the human-capital account of Chapter 10: if acquiring valuable skill is costly and takes years, _something_ must make people willing to pay that cost, and reward is the obvious candidate. And it captures an intuition most people share in practice even if they resist it in theory, that we do, in fact, expect to pay more for a skilled surgeon than an untrained one, and that the prospect of reward really does motivate real effort and real training. The functionalist account is not a cynical apology for privilege; in its strongest form it is a serious claim that inequality does identifiable work, and that a society ignoring this does so at its peril.

### 18.2 The Tumin critique, stated fairly

The Davis-Moore thesis provoked one of the most famous critiques in the history of sociology, from Melvin Tumin (1953), and the discipline of this book requires that we state Tumin's objections at _their_ full strength too, without conflating them with the thesis or mis-crediting who said what. Tumin did not simply dislike the functionalist conclusion; he raised specific, serious problems with the argument's logic, and they have force.

First, Tumin questioned the notion of "functional importance." How do we actually decide which positions are more important? The thesis treats this as obvious, but it is not. Is a surgeon more functionally important than the sanitation worker whose labor prevents epidemics, or the farm worker who grows the food? A society could not survive without either. The claim that some positions are objectively "more important" often turns out, on inspection, to smuggle in the existing hierarchy's own valuation, rewarding the positions that are _already_ highly rewarded and calling that importance, which makes the argument partly circular: the positions are important because they are rewarded, and rewarded because they are important.

Second, Tumin pointed out that the thesis ignores how _power_ shapes rewards. Rewards may attach to positions not because the positions are functionally important or hard to fill, but because the people in them have the _power_ to command high rewards, to restrict entry to their occupations, to set their own compensation, to protect their advantages. On this view, much of what the functionalist reads as "incentive for important work" is better read as the ability of the advantaged to extract rewards regardless of function, a reading that points toward the conflict tradition we will meet next.

Third, and this is Tumin's deepest point, stratification may be _dysfunctional_ as well as functional, and the thesis only counts the functions. Inequality, Tumin argued, restricts the discovery and development of talent: if reward and opportunity are unequally distributed, then talented people born to the lower rungs may never get the training the thesis assumes reward will call forth, so inequality _wastes_ talent rather than efficiently allocating it. This is a sharp internal objection, because it uses the thesis's own logic against it: if the goal is to get the most capable people into the most important positions, then an inequality steep enough to deny opportunity to the talented poor _defeats_ that goal. Inequality, beyond some point, may sort by birth rather than by talent, which is a dysfunction by the functionalist's own standard. (Notice this connects straight to the mobility and cumulative-advantage findings of Parts 3 and 4: if position is sticky and advantage compounds, the "incentive" story competes with a "wasted talent" story, and which dominates is contested.)

#### Common Misconception

A frequent error is to treat the Davis-Moore thesis and the Tumin critique as a settled match with a known winner, usually with Tumin declared the victor in textbooks that lean critical, or, less often, with Davis-Moore treated as obvious common sense. Neither is right, and the even-handedness must be real here. Tumin's objections are powerful and have reshaped how the thesis is understood, _and_ they do not simply refute it; the functionalist can reply that even granting that "importance" is hard to measure and that power distorts rewards, _some_ relationship between reward and the willingness to do demanding work plainly exists, or no one would endure long training, so the incentive function is real even if it is not the whole story and even if actual reward structures are distorted by power and waste talent. The honest state of the debate is that _both_ capture something: there probably is a real incentive function (Davis-Moore's insight) _and_ actual stratification is shaped heavily by power, partly circular in its definition of importance, and genuinely wasteful of talent (Tumin's insights), so that real-world inequality is some unknown mixture of functional incentive and dysfunctional power-driven extraction. Crowning either side is the error; mapping what each gets right is the work.

### 18.3 The conflict reframing

The functionalist and Tumin argue _within_ a shared frame: both ask whether inequality serves the society's needs. The conflict tradition, descending from Marx (Chapter 3) and sharpened by Weber's attention to power (Chapter 4), rejects the frame itself, and giving it its strongest form completes the picture.

The conflict theorist's core move is to deny that "society" has unified "needs" that stratification serves. Whose needs? A society is not a single organism with a common interest; it is an arena of _groups with conflicting interests_ , and the distribution of rewards reflects not the functional requirements of the whole but the _outcome of struggle_ between those groups, who has the power to claim what. On this account, the high rewards of advantaged positions are not incentives the society installed for its own good but advantages the powerful have secured and defended for _their_ good, and then dressed up, through ideology, as functionally necessary. The functionalist story, the conflict theorist says, is not just incomplete but _ideological_ : it is the kind of story a stratified society tells to make its inequality look like a benign necessity rather than the spoils of power, the very "production of the sense that the inequality is normal" we met in Chapter 1.

Stated at full strength, the conflict account is formidable. It explains why rewards so often track _power_ rather than any plausible measure of contribution (Tumin's second point, generalized into a whole framework). It explains why the advantaged work so hard to restrict entry, shape the rules, and propagate the belief that their position is deserved. And it fits the inheritance machinery of Part 3: if reward were purely a functional incentive for individual effort and training, why would it pass so reliably to children who have not yet done anything? The conflict theorist answers: because it was never mainly about function; it was about power, and power entrenches itself across generations.

But the conflict account has its own honest limits, and the discipline requires naming them. It can struggle to explain the genuine incentive effects the functionalist points to (why demanding training carries reward even in societies that tried to flatten hierarchy), risks treating _all_ reward differences as illegitimate power-extraction when some plausibly do track real contribution and scarcity, and, like any account that sees power everywhere, can become hard to falsify. The conflict frame is a powerful corrective to the functionalist's tendency to read the existing hierarchy as benign necessity; it is not, by itself, the whole truth either.

### 18.4 Function is not justice

Now the most important move in the chapter, the one that makes it the right opening to Part 7. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the functionalist were substantially right, that inequality really does serve important functions, really does motivate vital work, really is in some sense needed by a complex society. _Would that make it just?_ And the answer, which must be seen clearly, is: _not by itself._ Function is an IS-and-WHY matter (does inequality do useful work, and how?); justice is an OUGHT, and the one does not deliver the other.

Watch the gap. Even granting full functional necessity, a critic can press: necessary _for whom_ , and at _what cost to whom_? An arrangement can be functional for the smooth running of a society and still be unjust to those it places at the bottom, just as, in a grim historical analogy a conflict theorist might press, deeply unjust institutions have sometimes "worked" in the sense of being stable and productive. That an inequality is _useful_ does not settle that it is _deserved_ , or _fair_ , or that its costs are distributed acceptably. Conversely, from the other side: even if inequality were largely power-driven and only partly functional, that would not _automatically_ make it unjust either, since one would still need a value premise about why power-driven distributions are wrong. The functional question and the justice question are genuinely distinct, and this Part is about the second.

This is why "does society need inequality?" is the right first question of Part 7: not because its answer settles anything, but because working through it teaches the Part's governing lesson. The great normative debate ahead, meritocracy, Rawls and Nozick, opportunity versus outcome, is _not_ a debate about whether inequality is functional. It is a debate about whether, and under what conditions, inequality is _just_ , which is a different question that a functional analysis informs but cannot answer. Davis-Moore and Tumin and the conflict theorists have given us a rich picture of what inequality _does_. Whether what it does is _right_ is the question we now carry forward, still open, into the chapters on merit and justice.


### 18.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** State the Davis-Moore thesis at its strongest, and explain how it connects to the human-capital account of Chapter 10.

Hint

What problem does every society have to solve about filling positions, and how do unequal rewards solve it? If skill is costly to acquire, what must make people pay that cost?

**Answer:** The Davis-Moore thesis holds that stratification is _functionally necessary_ : a society must fill positions that differ in functional importance and in the talent/training they require, so it attaches _unequal rewards_ (income, prestige, privilege) to motivate capable people to seek the more important and demanding positions and to bear the costs of preparing for them. Unequal rewards are an _incentive mechanism_ ensuring vital work gets done; remove the incentive and the most demanding positions risk going unfilled or filled by the unprepared. It connects to Chapter 10's human-capital account directly: if acquiring valuable skill is costly and takes years, _something_ must make people willing to pay that cost, and reward is the obvious candidate, so the differential reward for skilled positions is the incentive that calls forth the costly investment in human capital. At its strongest the thesis is not a cynical apology but a serious claim that inequality does identifiable work, supported by the observation that demanding roles tend to carry greater rewards even across very different societies.

**Q2.** Give Tumin's three main criticisms of the Davis-Moore thesis, being careful to state them as objections to the _argument_ , not just expressions of dislike.

Hint

One is about how we decide "importance"; one is about power; one uses the thesis's own logic against it (wasted talent).

**Answer:** (1) _The problem of "functional importance"_ : the thesis assumes we can identify which positions are more important, but this is not obvious, a surgeon, a sanitation worker, and a farm worker are all indispensable, and claims of objective "importance" often smuggle in the existing hierarchy's own valuation, making the argument partly circular (positions are important because rewarded, rewarded because important). (2) _The role of power_ : rewards may attach to positions not because of function or scarcity but because occupants have the _power_ to command high rewards, restrict entry, and protect their advantages, so what looks like "incentive for important work" may be power-driven extraction. (3) _Dysfunction / wasted talent_ : stratification may be dysfunctional, not just functional, because unequal reward and opportunity mean talented people born low may never get the training the thesis assumes reward will call forth, so steep inequality _wastes_ talent and sorts by birth rather than ability, defeating the thesis's own stated goal (getting the most capable into the most important positions). The third is especially sharp because it turns the thesis's own logic against it. These are objections to the argument's validity, not mere distaste for its conclusion.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A defender of Davis-Moore says: "Even if Tumin is right that 'importance' is hard to measure and power distorts rewards, the basic incentive point still stands, no one would spend a decade training for a hard job for nothing." Evaluate this reply: does it rescue the thesis entirely, partly, or not at all? Use the chapter's "honest state of the debate."

Hint

Can the incentive function be real _and_ the actual reward structure be heavily distorted by power and wasteful of talent? Does conceding Tumin's points destroy the incentive point, or just bound it?

**Answer:** The reply rescues the thesis _partly_ , not entirely and not not-at-all. It is correct that conceding Tumin's points does not destroy the core incentive insight: _some_ real relationship between reward and the willingness to undertake costly training plainly exists, or no one would endure it, and this incentive function appears across very different societies, so it taps something genuine (the Davis-Moore insight survives). But it does not rescue the thesis _entirely_ , because Tumin's points still stand as limits: actual reward structures are shaped heavily by power (not just function), partly circular in defining "importance," and genuinely wasteful of talent when inequality denies opportunity to the talented poor. So the honest state of the debate is that real-world inequality is some unknown _mixture_ of functional incentive (real but not the whole story) and dysfunctional, power-driven extraction (real but not the whole story either). The reply correctly defends the existence of the incentive function while overreaching if it claims that function justifies the _actual_ reward structure, which is distorted in exactly the ways Tumin identified. Crowning either side is the error; the reply earns Davis-Moore a permanent seat at the table, not the head of it.

**Q2.** The conflict theorist asks: "If reward were purely a functional incentive for individual effort and training, why does it pass so reliably to children who haven't done anything yet?" Lay out the force of this question, then give the strongest reply available to a functionalist, and say why the chapter treats neither as decisive.

Hint

Inheritance (Part 3) is hard for a pure-incentive story to explain. But can a functionalist account for _some_ intergenerational transmission without abandoning the incentive point entirely?

**Answer:** _Force of the question_ : a pure incentive story says reward exists to motivate individuals to train and perform, but inherited advantage (Part 3) flows to children _before_ they have trained or performed anything, which the incentive logic cannot explain, why reward someone for effort not yet made? This fits the conflict reading that reward tracks _power_ (which entrenches across generations) rather than function, and it leverages the inheritance machinery of Part 3. _Strongest functionalist reply_ : the incentive function operates at the level of _positions and their rewards_ , and it can coexist with some intergenerational transmission, parents who earned rewards through the incentive system naturally use them to help their children (a separate phenomenon), and one can argue that allowing people to benefit their children is itself part of what makes the rewards motivating in the first place (people work partly _for_ their children). So inheritance does not refute the incentive function; it shows the system has effects beyond pure incentive. _Why neither is decisive_ : the conflict question genuinely wounds the _pure_ incentive story (reward clearly does more than incentivize individual effort, since it transmits), but it does not eliminate the incentive function (which still operates and still explains why demanding roles carry reward); meanwhile the functionalist reply concedes that inheritance exists and is not itself an incentive, which is a real concession to the conflict reading. The honest conclusion is that inheritance is better explained by the power/transmission account than by pure incentive, _and_ the incentive function is still real for the original earning, so both frameworks capture part of the truth, which is exactly why the chapter crowns neither.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter's pivotal claim is that "function is not justice", that even if inequality were fully functionally necessary, that would not by itself make it just. Test this hard. Construct the strongest argument that functional necessity _does_ bear on justice (so that a useful inequality has at least a claim to fairness), and the strongest argument that it does not. Where does the truth lie, and what value premise would you need to bridge function and justice?

**Discussion:** This question is the gateway to the entire normative Part, and working it carefully reveals exactly what kind of move the chapters on Rawls and Nozick will be making.

The strongest argument that function _does_ bear on justice: an inequality that genuinely makes everyone better off, including those at the bottom, by ensuring vital work gets done well, has a real claim to fairness that a purely arbitrary inequality lacks. If the differential reward to surgeons is what produces enough good surgeons to save lives, including the lives of the poor, then the inequality is not merely useful in the abstract but _useful to the very people it ranks lowest_ , and an arrangement that benefits everyone, even unequally, seems more defensible than one that benefits only the top. On this view, function bears on justice because a functional inequality can be a positive-sum arrangement, and it is hard to call unjust an inequality that leaves everyone, including the worst-off, better than they would be without it. (Notice this argument is a preview of one of the most influential moves in modern political philosophy, which Chapter 20 will name.)

The strongest argument that function does _not_ bear on justice: usefulness and fairness are simply different properties, and conflating them licenses real horrors. Many arrangements have been functional, stable, productive, smoothly self-perpetuating, and grossly unjust; that an institution "works" tells you nothing about whether it treats people fairly, since efficiency can be purchased at the price of injustice. Moreover, "functional necessity" arguments have a long history of being used to defend whatever hierarchy happens to exist, exactly the ideological move the conflict theorist warns of, so treating function as evidence of justice hands a blank check to the status quo. On this view, the justice of an inequality depends on considerations function cannot touch: whether those at the bottom consented, whether their position results from fair processes, whether their basic claims are met, whether the costs and benefits are distributed defensibly, none of which is answered by showing the arrangement is useful.

Where does the truth lie, and what bridges them? The key insight is that function bears on justice only _through a value premise_ , and which premise you accept determines how much function matters. If you accept something like "an inequality is just if it benefits everyone, including the worst-off" (a premise about mutual benefit), then functional necessity becomes highly relevant to justice, because functionality that lifts the bottom is exactly what that premise rewards. But if you accept instead "justice is about fair processes regardless of outcomes" or "justice requires meeting everyone's basic claims regardless of efficiency," then function is largely beside the point. So function and justice are bridged _only_ by a premise about what justice fundamentally requires, and that premise is itself contested, which is precisely why this is an OUGHT the book will not settle. The most defensible position is probably that functional necessity is _relevant but not sufficient_ : it can give an inequality a genuine claim to fairness _if_ you hold a mutual-benefit conception of justice and _if_ the inequality really does benefit the worst-off (an empirical condition often unmet, given the wasted-talent and power-extraction findings), but it cannot establish justice on its own, because reasonable people hold conceptions of justice on which usefulness is not the test. What this chapter has really done is show you that the move from "inequality is functional" to "inequality is just" requires a hidden premise about the nature of justice, and the next two chapters are precisely the laying-out of the competing premises, mutual benefit, fair process, desert, opportunity, outcome, that people actually use to make that move, each at full strength, none crowned. You now know what question you are really asking. Part 7 is the attempt to ask it well.

### Chapter Summary

Part 7 opened by calling due the OUGHT held in reserve for seventeen chapters: _is inequality just?_ We began with the most provocative answer, the functionalist **Davis-Moore thesis** , stated at full strength: because a society must fill positions differing in importance and in the talent/training they require, it attaches _unequal rewards_ as _incentives_ to motivate capable people into demanding roles and to bear the cost of preparing, so some inequality is a working feature of complex societies, not merely an accident or injustice. It connects to Chapter 10's human capital (costly skill needs a reward to call it forth) and captures the real intuition that reward motivates effort and training.

We stated **Tumin's critique** fairly and at full strength: the notion of "functional importance" is hard to define and often circular (importance smuggled in from existing rewards); _power_ , not function, may drive many rewards; and stratification can be _dysfunctional_ , wasting talent by denying opportunity to the talented poor, an objection that turns the thesis's own logic against it and connects to the mobility/cumulative-advantage findings. We refused to crown a winner: there probably _is_ a real incentive function (Davis-Moore) _and_ actual stratification is heavily shaped by power, partly circular, and wasteful of talent (Tumin), so real inequality is an unknown mixture of functional incentive and dysfunctional power-extraction.

The **conflict reframing** (from Marx and Weber) rejected the shared frame, denying that "society" has unified "needs": rewards reflect the _outcome of struggle_ between groups with conflicting interests, the high rewards of the advantaged are power secured and then dressed as necessity (ideology, Chapter 1's "production of the normal"), and the framing fits Part 3's inheritance machinery (why does reward pass to children who have done nothing?). We named its honest limits too (it can struggle with genuine incentive effects and risks seeing only power).

The chapter's pivotal lesson, and the right opening to Part 7: _function is not justice_. Even full functional necessity would not by itself make inequality just, because function is an IS/WHY matter and justice is an OUGHT, bridged only by a contested value premise about what justice requires (mutual benefit, fair process, desert, etc.). The Think Deeper showed exactly how that bridge works and which premise each side needs. We carry the question forward, still open, to Chapter 19's examination of **meritocracy** , the idea that inequality is just when it tracks merit, and its critics.

There is one idea about inequality that nearly everyone in a modern society holds, often without noticing they hold it, and it is this: that it is _fair_ for rewards to go to those who earn them through their own talent and effort, and _unfair_ for them to go by birth, connection, or accident. This is the ideal of **meritocracy** , rule by merit, reward by desert, and it is the moral default of the class society. It is what makes the rags-to-riches story inspiring (the riser _deserved_ it), what makes inherited privilege feel suspect (the heir did _not_ earn it), what we appeal to when we say a hire should go to the best candidate or a prize to the best work. If you feel the pull of any of those judgments, you are a partial meritocrat, and so is almost everyone you know.

Which makes it all the more startling to learn that the word "meritocracy" was coined, in the mid-twentieth century, as the name of a _dystopia_. The British writer who invented it, Michael Young, in his 1958 satire _The Rise of the Meritocracy_ , meant it satirically, as a warning about a society that sorted people ruthlessly by measured merit and then felt entitled to look down on those it sorted to the bottom. The word escaped its satirical origins and became a compliment, which is itself a fact worth pondering: the ideal we now treat as obviously good was first imagined as a nightmare. This chapter is about taking both the ideal and the nightmare seriously, steelmanning the case that meritocracy is the fairest principle we have _and_ the case that it is incoherent or even cruel, and holding the question open, because it is the hinge on which most people's intuitions about the justice of inequality actually turn.


### 19.1 The case for meritocracy, at full strength

Let us first give the meritocratic ideal its strongest and most attractive form, the version its serious defenders hold, not the caricature its critics attack.

#### Definition: Meritocracy

**Meritocracy** is the principle that social positions and rewards should be distributed according to _merit_ , usually understood as some combination of talent, ability, effort, and achievement, rather than according to birth, inherited status, connections, or group membership. As a normative ideal, it holds that an inequality is _just_ to the extent that it results from differences in merit fairly assessed, and _unjust_ to the extent that it results from morally arbitrary factors like the family one was born into.

In plain language: meritocracy says rewards should track what you _do and can do_ , not where you _came from_. State its appeal at full strength, because it is genuinely powerful and genuinely attractive across the political spectrum. First, the _fairness_ case: meritocracy is, at its core, an _anti-privilege_ principle. It is the idea that fired the great democratic revolutions against aristocracy, that careers should be open to talents, that a brilliant child of poor parents should be able to rise and a mediocre child of rich ones should not be guaranteed the top. Far from being a defense of the advantaged, meritocracy in its pure form is a _weapon against inherited advantage_ , which is why it has so often been the rallying cry of the excluded. Second, the _desert_ case: there is a deep and widely shared intuition that people _deserve_ the fruits of their own effort and talent, that someone who works hard and develops a valuable skill has a legitimate claim to the reward it earns, in a way that someone who merely inherited does not. Third, the _efficiency_ case, inherited from Chapter 18: matching the most capable people to the most demanding positions, and rewarding them for it, is good for everyone, including those at the bottom, because it means vital work is done by those best able to do it. A society that promoted by birth rather than merit would be both unjust _and_ worse-run.

Put together, the meritocratic ideal is formidable: it is anti-privilege, it honors effort and achievement, and it is efficient, and it captures intuitions that almost everyone shares in practice. When you are outraged that a job went to the boss's unqualified nephew rather than the talented applicant, you are a meritocrat. The ideal is not a fig leaf for the powerful; in its pure form it is the powerful's oldest enemy.

### 19.2 The case against, at full strength

Now the critique, given equal strength and equal vividness, because the discipline demands that the case against be as compelling as the case for, and because the critique of meritocracy is one of the most interesting bodies of thought in modern political philosophy.

The first and deepest criticism strikes at the concept of _merit_ itself: _is merit not, in large part, itself inherited?_ Everything in Parts 2 and 3 of this book presses this question. If the talents and dispositions that count as "merit", the cognitive abilities, the cultivated skills, the very capacity for sustained effort and deferred gratification, are themselves substantially products of the genetic and environmental lottery of birth (the inherited cultural capital of Chapter 9, the developed human capital of Chapter 10, the cumulative advantage of Chapter 7), then rewarding "merit" may be, at one remove, rewarding _birth_ after all, just laundered through a generation of development. The child who arrives at the meritocratic competition already advantaged, better prepared, more confident, healthier, better connected, and then "wins on merit," has won a race whose starting lines were set by exactly the inherited factors meritocracy claims to transcend. On this view, meritocracy does not _abolish_ the rule of birth; it _disguises_ it, converting inherited advantage into apparent desert and thereby making the resulting inequality feel earned when it was substantially given. This is the critique's sharpest edge: meritocracy may be the most effective legitimating ideology inherited privilege has ever found, precisely because it sincerely believes itself to be privilege's opposite.

The second criticism questions whether "desert" is even _coherent_ all the way down. Grant that effort deserves reward. But where does the _capacity_ for effort come from? If my ability to work hard is itself a product of my upbringing, my temperament, my health, factors I did not choose, then is my hard work really to my _credit_ in the deep sense desert requires? The philosopher's version of this question runs: to deserve X for doing Y, mustn't Y be genuinely _up to me_ , and if the qualities that let me do Y were themselves unearned gifts, does my desert not dissolve under inspection? This is a genuinely hard problem, and note that it threatens not only meritocracy but our ordinary sense of desert quite generally; we will not solve it, but a serious meritocrat must face it, because it suggests the "desert" at meritocracy's heart may rest on a notion of self-creation that no one actually satisfies.

The third criticism is the one Michael Young saw first, the _cruelty_ of a successful meritocracy. Suppose a society really did sort people perfectly by merit. Then those at the bottom could no longer tell themselves they were held down by an unfair system; they would have been told, with the full authority of a fair process, that they are simply _less meritorious_ , less able, less worthy. The aristocratic poor could at least blame the rigged game; the meritocratic poor are handed the verdict that they deserve their place. A perfect meritocracy, on this view, adds insult to inequality, stripping the unsuccessful of their dignity along with their share, and breeding in the successful a special arrogance, the belief that they owe their position to nothing but their own excellence and therefore owe the losers nothing. The nightmare Young named is a society that is fair by its own lights and merciless because of it.


#### Common Misconception

The error to avoid here, in both directions, is to mistake one of these for a knockout blow. On one side, critics sometimes treat the "merit is inherited" point as _refuting_ meritocracy entirely, as if showing that merit is partly inherited showed that effort and talent count for _nothing_ and all outcomes are pure birth. That overshoots: Chapter 10 established that real, developed ability and genuine effort _do_ exist and _do_ contribute, even if they are also shaped by inheritance, so meritocracy is _complicated_ by the inheritance of merit, not annihilated by it. On the other side, defenders sometimes treat the practical impossibility of _perfect_ meritocracy as irrelevant, as if the ideal were untouched by never being reached. That also overshoots: if real "merit" is always substantially inherited, then actual meritocratic competitions always partly reward birth, which is a serious problem for the ideal _in practice_ , not just in theory. The honest position holds both: merit is _real but substantially shaped by unchosen factors_ , so meritocracy is neither a pure fraud nor a clean ideal, but a principle whose application is permanently entangled with the inheritance it claims to overcome. How much that entanglement undercuts it is exactly the contested question.

### 19.3 Why the question will not resolve

We have two formidable cases. Meritocracy is the great anti-privilege ideal, honoring effort and achievement and serving efficiency, the oldest enemy of inherited aristocracy. And meritocracy is a potential disguise for inherited advantage, resting on a notion of desert that may not survive inspection, and threatening, if ever perfected, a special cruelty toward those it sorts to the bottom. Both are serious. Neither refutes the other. Why does the question not resolve?

Because, at bottom, the disagreement rests on contested value premises that the facts cannot settle, exactly the structure this book has traced throughout. Consider what the two sides would need to agree on to agree about meritocracy, and notice that each is a genuine open question.

They would need to agree on _what counts as merit_ , and whether merit that is substantially inherited still grounds desert. This is partly the coherence-of-desert problem, a deep and unresolved question in moral philosophy on which reasonable people genuinely differ. Some hold that you can deserve the fruits of qualities you did not ultimately create (it is enough that they are _yours_ and you exercised them); others hold that desert requires a self-creation no one achieves. The facts of Parts 2 and 3 (that merit is substantially inherited) are settled enough; what they _imply for desert_ is a value question they cannot answer.

They would need to agree on _what justice is fundamentally about_ , whether it is about _process_ (was the competition fair?) or _outcome_ (how do the losers fare?). A process-focused person can accept that meritocracy sorts people unequally and still call it just _if_ the sorting was fair; an outcome-focused person can accept that the sorting was fair and still call the result unjust _if_ the losers are left destitute or stripped of dignity. Young's cruelty critique only bites if you care about the _condition_ of the losers, not only the _fairness_ of the process, and whether you do is a value commitment, not a finding. (This is the opportunity-versus-outcome question that Chapter 20 will make central.)

So the meritocracy debate, like every debate in Part 7, turns out to rest on contested premises about desert and about the nature of justice, and the book's job is the same as always: to lay out the strongest cases, to show you exactly which value questions your verdict depends on, and to hand you the verdict. If you came to this chapter a confident meritocrat, you should leave it still able to defend the ideal but now aware that it rests on a contestable theory of desert and that its perfection might be a nightmare. If you came a confident critic, you should leave still able to press the critique but now aware that you cannot do so without affirming the reality of effort and talent and without a value premise about why fair process is not enough. That is not the dissatisfaction of a question dodged. It is the achievement of a question finally seen whole.

### 19.4 Toward the philosophers

We have been doing political philosophy in this chapter without quite admitting it, and it is time to admit it, because the meritocracy debate leads directly to the most rigorous statements of the rival theories of distributive justice that the whole Part has been circling. The questions that made meritocracy irresolvable, _what is justice fundamentally about, process or outcome? do we deserve the fruits of unchosen gifts? what do we owe those at the bottom?_ , are exactly the questions that two twentieth-century philosophers, John Rawls and Robert Nozick, addressed with more care and rigor than anyone before or since. They reached opposite conclusions, and the clash between them is the sharpest available statement of the choice every reader must make for themselves. Chapter 20 gives each his strongest form: Rawls, who argued that justice requires arranging inequalities to benefit the least advantaged, and Nozick, who argued that justice is about how holdings came to be, not how they are distributed. Between them lies the contested heart of the contested heart, and once you have seen both at full strength, you will have everything the book can give you for thinking about whether inequality is just, except the answer, which was never the book's to give.
