#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Almost everyone is a "partial meritocrat", outraged when a job goes to the boss's unqualified nephew, yet most people also feel a parent helping their own child is acceptable (Chapter 8). But the nephew case _is_ a parent helping their child. What distinction are people actually drawing, and can it be made principled? Use this to explore what, if anything, a defensible version of meritocracy would require.

**Discussion:** This is a wonderful question because it exposes a tension most people carry unexamined, and working it out reveals what a defensible meritocracy might actually look like.

Start with the puzzle. Nearly everyone condemns the boss hiring his unqualified nephew over a better candidate, that feels like a paradigm violation of meritocratic fairness. Yet nearly everyone also accepts a parent paying for tutoring, funding college, providing a stable home, all of which are _also_ parents helping their children gain advantage (Chapter 8). If both are "parents helping children," why does one feel like corruption and the other like love? People are clearly drawing a distinction; the question is whether it is principled or merely convenient.

Several candidate distinctions, each with force and each with problems. One: the nephew case involves a _direct, zero-sum_ transfer of a specific position away from a more deserving person, while tutoring builds _general capacities_. But this is shakier than it looks, because the tutored child _also_ eventually takes specific positions away from less-tutored, possibly more talented children; the harm is just more diffuse and deferred, which may make it less _visible_ without making it less _real_ (recall Chapter 9 on how cumulative advantage works invisibly). Two: the nephew case rewards advantage _without developing real merit_ , while tutoring _develops_ genuine ability, so the tutored child really is more capable. This is more principled, it locates the wrong in rewarding _unearned and undeveloped_ advantage, while allowing advantage that produces real merit, but it runs straight into Chapter 19's central problem: if the developed merit is itself bought by advantage, the distinction between "developing real merit" and "buying position" blurs, since both convert parental resources into the child's competitive edge. Three: the nephew case violates an _explicit fair-competition norm_ (the hiring was supposed to be open and merit-based), while family investment operates _before and outside_ such competitions. This may be the distinction people are actually drawing: we accept advantage-building in the private sphere of the family but demand merit-only rules within designated competitions (hiring, admissions). It is somewhat principled, but it has the uncomfortable implication that meritocracy is fair _only within_ arenas whose entrants were shaped by profoundly unequal private advantage, which is exactly the "fair race, unfair starting lines" problem.

What does this reveal about a defensible meritocracy? Probably this: pure meritocracy, "reward merit, period", is unstable, because merit is built by the very inherited advantages meritocracy condemns, so a thoroughgoing meritocrat would have to object to family advantage itself, which almost no one is willing to do (Chapter 8's tension between fair life chances and the value of the family). A defensible version therefore has to be _bounded and honest_ : it can insist on merit-only rules _within_ specific competitions (no nephews) while acknowledging that this does not deliver full fairness because the competitors arrived unequally prepared, and it can support efforts to _equalize the starting lines_ (the development of merit) without pretending the competition itself is the whole of justice. Such a meritocracy is more modest than the triumphant version: it knows it is administering fair rules to an unfair race, and it does not award the winners the full moral credit that pure meritocracy would, because it knows their merit was partly given. Whether even this modest version is _just_ still depends on the contested premises this chapter identified, what we owe the losers, whether process-fairness suffices, whether developed merit grounds desert. But the exercise shows that most people's actual intuitions point toward this bounded, honest meritocracy rather than the pure version, and that the distinction they draw between the nephew and the tutor, while not perfectly principled, gestures at a real and defensible idea: that there is a difference between rigging a competition and preparing for one, even if inheritance makes that difference far blurrier than we like to admit. Where you finally land is, as ever, yours to decide, but you now decide it knowing what the question really is.

### Chapter Summary

We examined **meritocracy** , the moral default of the class society, the principle that positions and rewards should track _merit_ (talent, ability, effort, achievement) rather than birth, connection, or group, with an inequality just insofar as it reflects fairly assessed merit. We noted the irony that the word was coined (by Michael Young) to name a _dystopia_ and became a compliment, and we steelmanned the ideal at full strength: it is anti-privilege (the oldest enemy of inherited aristocracy, the rallying cry of the excluded), it honors desert (people deserve the fruits of their effort and talent), and it serves efficiency (matching the capable to demanding roles benefits all). Almost everyone is a partial meritocrat.

We gave the critique equal strength: that _merit is itself substantially inherited_ (the talents and even the capacity for effort are shaped by the lottery of birth, Chapters 7, 9, 10), so meritocracy may _disguise_ rather than abolish the rule of birth, the most effective legitimating ideology privilege ever found; that _desert may be incoherent_ all the way down (if the capacity for effort is unchosen, is the effort to one's credit?); and that a _successful meritocracy could be cruel_ (Young's warning: the meritocratic poor are told they _deserve_ the bottom, stripped of the dignity the aristocratic poor could keep). We held that these _complicate_ rather than _annihilate_ meritocracy: merit is real but substantially shaped by unchosen factors, so meritocracy is neither pure fraud nor clean ideal.

The question will not resolve because it rests on contested value premises the facts cannot settle: _what counts as merit and whether inherited merit grounds desert_ (the coherence-of-desert problem), and _whether justice is about process or outcome_ (Young's cruelty critique bites only for those who care about the losers' condition, not only the fairness of the process). The Think Deeper used the nephew-versus-tutor puzzle to show most people's intuitions point toward a _bounded, honest_ meritocracy that administers fair rules while acknowledging the race's unequal starting lines, rather than the triumphant pure version.

These very questions, process versus outcome, desert and unchosen gifts, what we owe the worst-off, lead directly to Chapter 20's rigorous statements of rival theories of distributive justice: **Rawls** , who argued inequalities must benefit the least advantaged, and **Nozick** , who argued justice is about how holdings arose, not how they are distributed. Their clash is the sharpest statement of the choice every reader must make.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
We have reached the sharpest point of the whole book, the place where the question "is inequality just?" receives its two most rigorous and most opposed answers. They come from two philosophers writing in the same university in the same era, Nozick's book written in explicit, admiring response to Rawls's, and they reached conclusions about as far apart as serious thought can travel. John Rawls, in _A Theory of Justice_ (1971), argued that a just society arranges its inequalities to benefit the least advantaged. Robert Nozick, in _Anarchy, State, and Utopia_ (1974), argued that whether a distribution is just has nothing to do with how it benefits anyone, and everything to do with how it came about. Each built his case with a care that has not been surpassed, and the clash between them is the clearest available map of the choice every reader of this book must, in the end, make alone.

This chapter is the climax of Part 7, and its discipline is the book's discipline at maximum stakes: to give each philosopher his _strongest and most accurate_ form, the version his own followers would recognize and his honest opponents would respect, and to crown neither. Both are routinely caricatured, Rawls into "redistribute everything," Nozick into "let the rich keep their money", and both caricatures are worse than useless, because the actual arguments are far subtler and far more interesting than the slogans, and because you cannot make your own honest choice between positions you have only met as cartoons. We will state each as he meant it, set them against each other, and then frame the underlying choice, between justice as _fair process_ and justice as _fair outcome_ , that the whole Part has been building toward, and hand it to you.


### 20.1 Rawls: justice as fairness

John Rawls asked a question of disarming simplicity: what principles for the basic structure of society would people choose if they had to choose _fairly_? And he proposed a famous thought experiment to model fair choosing.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Definition: The Original Position and the Veil of Ignorance

Rawls's **original position** is a hypothetical situation in which people choose the basic principles of their society from behind a **veil of ignorance** : they do not know who they will be in that society, their class, talents, race, sex, wealth, or conception of the good. Stripped of knowledge of their own position, they cannot rig the principles to favor themselves, so whatever they would agree to is, Rawls argued, _fair_ , because it was chosen without bias toward any particular position.

In plain language: imagine designing the rules of a society you will then have to live in, _without knowing where in it you will land_ , top or bottom, gifted or struggling. The veil of ignorance is a device for forcing impartiality: since you might end up anywhere, you cannot privilege the position you happen to occupy, because you do not know what it is. Rawls argued that rational people choosing under these conditions would, being unwilling to gamble their whole lives on landing at the top, choose principles that protect against ending up at the bottom. And he argued they would choose, in a specific order, a set of principles, the ordering being essential and almost always lost in popular accounts.

_First_ , and lexically prior to everything else, they would choose equal basic _liberties_ for all, freedom of speech, conscience, person, political participation, secured first and not tradeable for material gain. _Second_ , and only after liberty is secured, they would choose two things governing social and economic inequalities: that positions be open to all under _fair equality of opportunity_ , and that inequalities be arranged to the greatest benefit of the _least advantaged_. This last is the famous **difference principle** , and stating it in its proper place is crucial.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Definition: The Difference Principle (in its proper order)

Rawls's **difference principle** holds that social and economic inequalities are just _only if_ they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. It is _not_ a demand for equal outcomes, and it is _not_ Rawls's whole theory: it applies only _after_ equal basic liberties are secured (the first principle, which takes priority) and _alongside_ fair equality of opportunity. Within those constraints, the difference principle permits inequalities, even large ones, _provided_ they make the worst-off better off than they would be under any more equal arrangement.

In plain language: Rawls does not say inequality is bad, or that everyone must have the same. He says inequality is _justified to the extent that it helps those at the bottom_. If paying surgeons more, or letting entrepreneurs grow rich, actually improves the lives of the least advantaged (better medicine, more jobs, more innovation that reaches everyone), then that inequality is just by the difference principle. If an inequality does _not_ benefit the worst-off, if it merely concentrates advantage at the top while the bottom gains nothing, then it fails the test. Notice how subtle and how far from "redistribute everything" this is. Rawls _permits_ inequality, sometimes substantial inequality, but sets a condition: it must earn its keep by lifting the floor. The test is not "is everyone equal?" but "are the worst-off as well-off as they could be?" This is why the difference principle is best read not as egalitarian leveling but as a demand that inequality _justify itself to those it ranks lowest_ , which connects directly to the functionalist argument of Chapter 18: a Davis-Moore inequality that genuinely benefits everyone including the bottom could _pass_ the difference principle, while one that is mere power-extraction would fail it. Rawls gives the "function is not justice" worry a precise resolution: function bears on justice exactly insofar as it benefits the least advantaged.

The deep engine of Rawls's view, and its most contested premise, is his treatment of the natural and social lottery. The talents you are born with, and the family that develops them, are, Rawls insists, _morally arbitrary_ , you did nothing to deserve them. So the distribution of income and wealth that flows from those arbitrary advantages has, in itself, no claim to be _deserved_. This does not mean talents should be ignored; it means a just society treats the distribution of talents as a _common asset_ , arranging things so that the lucky may profit from their gifts only on terms that also benefit the unlucky. This is the philosophical heart of the structural side of Thread C, given its most rigorous form: if merit is substantially inherited (Chapter 19), then the rewards of merit are not fully deserved, and justice requires that they be arranged to help those who drew shorter straws.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
### 20.2 Nozick: justice as entitlement

Robert Nozick rejected this entire approach, and his counter is as rigorous as Rawls's and aimed precisely at its foundation. His objection is not that helping the worst-off is bad, but that Rawls is asking the _wrong question_. Justice, Nozick argued, is not about achieving any particular _pattern_ of distribution at all, not equality, not the difference principle, not any end-state. (Nozick's own terms for what he opposes are "patterned" and "end-state" theories; this book calls the same target "structural" to tie it into Thread C, but the original vocabulary is his.) It is about whether the _process_ by which holdings came to be was just.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Nozick's Entitlement Theory

Nozick's **entitlement theory** holds that a distribution of holdings is just if and only if it arose by just steps, regardless of the resulting pattern. It has three principles: **just acquisition** (how unowned things may justly come to be owned), **just transfer** (holdings justly acquired may be justly transferred through voluntary exchange and gift), and **rectification** (past injustices in acquisition or transfer must be corrected). If your holdings came to you through just acquisition and a chain of just transfers, you are _entitled_ to them, whatever the overall distribution looks like, and no one may take them to achieve a preferred pattern.

In plain language: Nozick says justice is _historical_ , not _structural_. Do not ask "is this distribution fair?" (a snapshot question); ask "did this distribution come about by fair steps?" (a history question). If every step was just, each person acquiring justly and transferring voluntarily, then the result is just _however unequal it is_ , because it is nothing but the sum of free choices no one had the right to forbid. This is emphatically _not_ merely "opposition to redistribution," and reading it that way misses the argument's real force. Nozick's claim is about the _nature of justice itself_ : that imposing any preferred pattern necessarily means _overriding the free choices_ through which people justly came to have what they have, and that doing so treats people's holdings, and ultimately people themselves, as resources to be arranged by others rather than as free agents entitled to what they justly earned and were freely given.

Nozick's sharpest argument against pattern-based theories like Rawls's is worth reconstructing, because it is genuinely powerful. Suppose you achieve your favorite distribution, perfectly equal, or perfectly Rawlsian. Now suppose many people each freely choose to pay a small amount to watch a uniquely talented performer, who thereby grows rich. The new distribution is unequal, but it arose entirely from voluntary choices people had every right to make, each giving a little of what was justly theirs to someone they wished to give it to. To restore the original pattern, you would have to _forbid_ those voluntary exchanges or _confiscate_ the proceeds, that is, interfere with people's freedom to do as they like with what is justly theirs. So, Nozick argues, _maintaining any pattern requires continuous interference with liberty_ , and since the exchanges were just at every step, the resulting inequality is just, and the interference is what would be unjust. Patterned justice, on this view, is incompatible with freedom, because free people will always disturb any pattern, and only constant coercion could restore it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
Note crucially that Nozick's theory contains its _own_ radical critique of existing inequality, through the rectification principle, which is almost always forgotten. If actual holdings trace back to _unjust_ acquisition (theft, conquest, fraud, expropriation) or unjust transfer, then the entitlement theory does _not_ bless the current distribution; it demands _rectification_ of those past injustices. A Nozickian who took the historical record seriously could end up endorsing dramatic correction of holdings whose lineage is tainted, which connects directly to the historical-legacy account of the wealth gap in Chapter 17. Nozick is not a defender of the status quo; he is a defender of _justly acquired_ holdings, and whether actual holdings are justly acquired is a historical question his own theory makes central.


### 20.3 The clash, and the choice beneath it

Set them side by side. For Rawls, an inequality is just if it benefits the least advantaged, because the talents that produce it are morally arbitrary and undeserved. For Nozick, an inequality is just if it arose through just acquisition and free transfer, because people are entitled to the fruits of their liberty regardless of the resulting pattern. These are not two answers to the same question; they are, at bottom, two different _theories of what justice is about_ , and seeing the choice beneath them is the climax of the entire book.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Definition: Justice as Outcome vs. Justice as Process

**Justice as outcome** (or end-state, patterned) holds that the justice of a distribution depends on the _resulting state of affairs_ , how people fare, especially the worst-off (Rawls's difference principle is one version). **Justice as process** (or historical, procedural) holds that the justice of a distribution depends on _how it came about_ , whether the steps were fair, regardless of the resulting pattern (Nozick's entitlement theory is one version). The deepest disagreements about inequality often turn out to be disagreements about which of these justice fundamentally _is_.

In plain language: is a just distribution one with a fair _result_ , or one produced by a fair _procedure_? This is the fork the whole book has been approaching. Almost every argument about the justice of inequality, the meritocracy debate of Chapter 19, the cruelty critique, the wealth-gap verdicts of Chapter 17, reduces, when pressed, to where a person stands on this fork. The process-focused person can accept a very unequal outcome as just if it arose fairly, and will see attempts to correct it as violations of liberty. The outcome-focused person can accept constraints on liberty as just if they produce a fairer result, and will see an unequal outcome as unjust however it arose. They are not disagreeing about facts. They are disagreeing about what the word "just" fundamentally _means_ , and this is a value disagreement that no amount of evidence can resolve.

And here, at the sharpest point, the book does what it has promised to do throughout: it declines to choose for you. Both Rawls and Nozick built rigorous, honest, internally coherent theories from premises that millions of thoughtful people find compelling. The choice between them, between justice as fair outcome and justice as fair process, is not a choice the facts can make, not a choice the experts can make for you, and not a choice this book will make. It is the deepest of the contested OUGHTs, and it is yours. What the book _can_ do, and has tried to do, is ensure that whichever way you lean, you lean _knowingly_ : able to state the other side so its adherents would nod, aware that your own position rests on a contestable premise about the nature of justice, and freed from the comfortable illusion that the question has an obvious answer that only the wicked or the foolish could miss. There is no such answer. There are two great traditions, each capturing something real, and a choice that respects your intelligence precisely by refusing to make it for you.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
### 20.4 Opportunity, outcome, and what remains

Most people, pressed, do not land cleanly on either pole. They want _something_ of both: a society where outcomes arise from fair processes _and_ where the worst-off are not abandoned, where liberty is real _and_ where the starting lines are not grotesquely unequal. This instinct toward the middle is not muddle; it is the recognition that both traditions capture something true, and most actual political positions are attempts to weight the two. The popular distinction between _equality of opportunity_ (everyone gets a fair chance; outcomes may differ) and _equality of outcome_ (the results themselves should be more equal) is the everyday version of the Rawls-Nozick fork, and it inherits the same irreducible contest, because "fair chance" smuggles in outcome questions (how fair can the chance be if the starting lines, set by inheritance, are wildly unequal?), and "equal outcome" smuggles in process questions (equalized how, at what cost to liberty?). Even the comfortable middle, on inspection, does not dissolve the choice; it only requires you to make it in degrees rather than absolutes.

We have now laid out the contested heart in full. The functionalist asks whether inequality is _needed_ (Chapter 18); the meritocrat asks whether it tracks _desert_ (Chapter 19); Rawls and Nozick ask whether justice is about _outcome_ or _process_ (this chapter). Each is a genuine question, each has its strongest answers, and none has been settled here, because none can be settled by anything but a reader's own reasoned value judgment. This is not the book failing to do its job. It is the book doing exactly the job it set itself in Chapter 2: to separate what is measured from what is contested from what is a question of values, and, having taken you as far as evidence and argument can go, to hand you the verdict that was always yours to make.

One Part remains. We have examined inequality _within_ a society from every angle, measured, mechanical, mobile, lived, grouped, and judged. Chapter 21 widens the frame to inequality _between_ nations, the global stratification that dwarfs in scale anything within a single society, and Chapter 22 closes the book by turning to the contested "consequences of inequality" and, finally, to the honest open questions you now carry, including the strange discomfort of seeing the ladder clearly without being told what to do about it. The verdict is yours. The last Part is about learning to live with having to make it.


### 20.5 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** State Rawls's difference principle _in its proper place_ , and explain why "redistribute everything" is a caricature of it.

Hint

What two things come _before_ the difference principle in Rawls's ordering? And does the principle forbid inequality, or set a condition on it?

**Answer:** The difference principle holds that social and economic inequalities are just _only if_ they work to the greatest benefit of the _least advantaged_. In its proper place, it is _not_ Rawls's whole theory and _not_ first: it applies only _after_ equal basic liberties are secured (the lexically prior first principle) and _alongside_ fair equality of opportunity. "Redistribute everything" is a caricature because the difference principle does _not_ demand equal outcomes, it _permits_ inequalities, even large ones, _provided_ they make the worst-off better off than they would be under any more equal arrangement. If paying surgeons more or letting entrepreneurs grow rich genuinely improves the lives of the least advantaged, that inequality is _just_ by the difference principle; it fails only when inequality concentrates advantage at the top while the bottom gains nothing. So the principle is best read as a demand that inequality _justify itself to those it ranks lowest_ , not as egalitarian leveling, which is why it can even bless a Davis-Moore inequality that truly benefits everyone (Chapter 18).

**Q2.** Explain why Nozick's entitlement theory is "historical, not structural," and why "opposition to redistribution" is an inadequate summary of it. Be sure to include the rectification principle.

Hint

Does Nozick ask whether a distribution's _pattern_ is fair, or whether its _history_ was just? And what does his theory demand if holdings trace to past theft or conquest?

**Answer:** Nozick's theory is _historical_ because it judges a distribution by _how it came about_ , not by its resulting _pattern_ (structure). A distribution is just if and only if it arose by just steps: **just acquisition** (how unowned things justly become owned), **just transfer** (voluntary exchange and gift), and **rectification** (correcting past injustices). If holdings came through just acquisition and a chain of just transfers, the holder is _entitled_ to them _whatever the pattern looks like_. "Opposition to redistribution" is inadequate for two reasons. First, it misses that the theory is fundamentally about the _nature of justice_ (justice is process, and imposing any pattern overrides the free choices through which people justly acquired things, treating them as resources to be arranged). Second, and crucially, the _rectification_ principle gives the theory its own radical critique of existing inequality: if actual holdings trace to _unjust_ acquisition (theft, conquest, fraud, expropriation) or unjust transfer, the theory does _not_ bless the current distribution but _demands_ correction, which connects to the historical-legacy account of the wealth gap (Chapter 17). Nozick defends _justly acquired_ holdings, not the status quo, and whether actual holdings are justly acquired is a historical question his theory makes central.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Reconstruct Nozick's argument that "maintaining any pattern requires continuous interference with liberty" (the talented-performer example), then give the strongest Rawlsian reply.

Hint

Start from any preferred distribution; let people freely pay to watch a performer. What happens to the pattern, and what would restoring it require? Then: can a Rawlsian question whether the "starting" distribution and the "free" choices are as clean as the argument assumes?

**Answer:** _Nozick's argument_ : Start from any preferred distribution (say, perfectly equal, or Rawlsian). Now suppose many people each freely pay a small sum to watch a uniquely talented performer, who thereby grows rich. The new distribution is unequal, but it arose _entirely_ from voluntary choices people had every right to make, each giving a little of what was justly theirs. To restore the original pattern, you would have to _forbid_ those exchanges or _confiscate_ the proceeds, interfering with people's liberty to do as they wish with what is justly theirs. So maintaining _any_ pattern requires _continuous_ interference with liberty, and since each step was just, the resulting inequality is just and the interference is what is unjust; patterned justice is incompatible with freedom. _Strongest Rawlsian reply_ : the argument assumes the _initial_ holdings were already just and the choices _fully_ free, but a Rawlsian questions both. The "small sums" people spend come from holdings that themselves flowed from the morally arbitrary lottery of talent and birth, so they are not unconditionally "theirs" to begin with; and Rawls's principles govern the _basic structure_ (the background rules within which exchanges occur), not each individual transaction, so a just background structure (including taxation) is not a series of objectionable interferences with particular free choices but the fair framework that makes the choices fair in the first place. On this reply, taxing the performer's gains to maintain just background conditions no more violates liberty than the rules of a fair game violate the players' freedom; it is the condition of the game being fair. Whether you find Nozick's "every step was just, so the result is just" or Rawls's "the background structure must be just for the steps to count as fair" more compelling depends on the process-versus-outcome fork, which the chapter leaves to you.

**Q2.** A person says: "I believe in equality of opportunity, not equality of outcome." Using the chapter's claim that this distinction "inherits the same irreducible contest," show how their position smuggles in outcome questions it cannot avoid.

Hint

How "fair" can the _opportunity_ be if the starting lines are set by inherited advantage (Parts 2-3)? Can you secure genuine equality of opportunity without affecting outcomes?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src: **Answer:** The position sounds like a clean choice for process over outcome, but "equality of _opportunity_ " cannot be cashed out without confronting outcomes. The problem: a genuinely _fair chance_ requires _fair starting lines_ , but starting lines are set by inherited advantage, the wealth, schooling, neighborhoods, networks, and cultural capital of Parts 2-3, which are _outcomes_ of the previous generation. So if you take equality of opportunity seriously, you must ask how the children's _opportunities_ can be equal when their parents' _outcomes_ were wildly unequal and those outcomes shape the children's starting positions. To secure real equality of opportunity, you would have to intervene in the transmission of advantage (affecting outcomes), and if you refuse to (leaving inherited advantage intact), then the "opportunity" you offer is fair only in a thin, formal sense (no legal barriers) while remaining substantively unequal (vastly different starting lines). Either way, outcome questions reappear: either you accept that "equal opportunity" is merely formal and tolerates large substantive unfairness, or you find yourself equalizing starting lines, which means shaping outcomes. The distinction therefore does not let you escape the Rawls-Nozick fork; it relocates it. "Fair chance" smuggles in outcome questions (how fair can the chance be given unequal starting lines?), just as "equal outcome" smuggles in process questions (equalized how, at what cost to liberty?). The honest version of the position must specify _how much_ substantive equalizing of starting lines it requires, which is a matter of degree on the same contested fork, not a clean alternative to it.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** This chapter says the choice between Rawls and Nozick is, at bottom, a choice between justice as _outcome_ and justice as _process_ , and that it "is yours" to make. But is the choice really binary? Construct a position that takes something essential from _each_ , and then honestly assess: does such a hybrid dissolve the disagreement, or does it just relocate the hard choice? What does this tell you about why the book refuses to deliver a verdict?

**Discussion:** This is the capstone of the entire normative Part, and it rewards resisting both the urge to pick a pole and the urge to think a hybrid escapes the problem.

First, the hybrid, which most reflective people and most actual societies gesture toward. One can hold that _process matters_ (people are entitled to the fruits of genuinely free choices, coercion requires justification, liberty is a real value Nozick rightly defends) _and_ that _outcomes matter_ (a society that lets people starve or strips the worst-off of dignity is unjust however its distribution arose, Rawls's concern for the least advantaged is real). Such a hybrid might say: secure robust liberties and honor voluntary exchange (a nod to Nozick), _within_ a background structure that guarantees everyone a decent minimum and fair-enough starting lines (a nod to Rawls). This is, roughly, the position of many actual mixed economies, and it is not incoherent; it reflects the genuine insight that _both_ traditions captured something true, which is exactly what this book has insisted throughout.

But does the hybrid _dissolve_ the disagreement? No, and seeing why is the real lesson. The hybrid does not eliminate the hard choice; it _relocates_ it to the question of _how to weight the two_ and _where to set the dials_. How robust must liberty be before it may be constrained for the sake of the worst-off? How decent a minimum, how fair the starting lines, before the duty to outcomes is satisfied and liberty resumes priority? Every actual political disagreement in a mixed society, about taxation, inheritance, education funding, redistribution, is a disagreement about _where to set these dials_ , and the dials are set by exactly the value weighting the pure theories made vivid. The hybrid does not answer "process or outcome?"; it answers "both," and then immediately faces "how much of each, and which wins when they conflict?", which is the same contested choice in a new form. The person who says "I want both liberty and a fair floor" has not escaped the fork; they have committed to walking along it, and where they stop is still a value judgment no fact can make for them.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src: What does this tell you about why the book refuses a verdict? It tells you the refusal is not evasion or cowardice but _accuracy_. The book refuses to deliver a verdict because there genuinely is no verdict that evidence or argument can compel: the choice, whether to pick a pole or to set the dials of a hybrid, rests finally on contested premises about the nature of justice (process versus outcome, the moral weight of liberty versus the claims of the worst-off, whether unchosen talents ground desert) on which reasonable, informed, good-faith people permanently disagree. A book that delivered a verdict would not be wiser than its readers; it would simply be _imposing its author's value weighting_ and disguising it as a conclusion, which is precisely the verdict-by-disguise the whole book has taught you to detect. The refusal honors two things at once: the genuine difficulty of the question (it is hard because it really is hard, not because we have not thought enough), and the reader's standing as a moral agent entitled to make their own reasoned judgment about the deepest of all the contested OUGHTs. You have now seen the strongest cases the great traditions offer. The weighting is yours. That it is yours, and not the book's, is not the book running out of things to say; it is the book keeping its central promise, made all the way back in Chapter 1, to help you see the question in its full difficulty and to respect your right to your own conclusion. The verdict was always going to be yours. The book's work was to make sure that when you reach it, you reach it with both eyes open.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 20: Rawls, Nozick, and the Justice of Holdings
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

We reached the climax of Part 7: the two most rigorous and opposed answers to "is inequality just?" **Rawls** asked what principles people would choose from behind a **veil of ignorance** (not knowing their own position), and argued they would choose, _in order_ : equal basic liberties first (lexically prior), then fair equality of opportunity together with the **difference principle** , that inequalities are just _only if_ they benefit the _least advantaged_. We stressed the proper ordering and that this is _not_ "redistribute everything": it permits even large inequalities provided they lift the floor, demanding that inequality justify itself to those it ranks lowest, with its engine the claim that talents are _morally arbitrary_ and so their rewards not fully deserved (the rigorous form of Thread C's structural pole).

**Nozick** rejected the whole pattern-based approach: justice is _historical_ , not structural. His **entitlement theory** (just acquisition, just transfer, rectification) holds a distribution just if it arose by just steps, _whatever the resulting pattern_. We stressed this is _not_ mere "opposition to redistribution": it is a claim about the nature of justice (imposing any pattern overrides free choices), made vivid by the talented-performer argument (maintaining any pattern requires continuous interference with liberty), and it contains its own radical critique through _rectification_ (holdings tracing to past injustice demand correction, connecting to Chapter 17's historical-legacy account).

Beneath their clash lies the book's central fork: **justice as outcome** (the resulting state, especially the worst-off, matters, Rawls) versus **justice as process** (how it came about matters, regardless of pattern, Nozick). Almost every argument about inequality reduces, when pressed, to where one stands here, and it is a _value_ disagreement no evidence can resolve. The everyday version, _equality of opportunity_ versus _equality of outcome_ , inherits the same contest (each smuggles in the other), so even the comfortable middle only requires making the choice in degrees. The Think Deeper showed that a Rawls-Nozick _hybrid_ does not dissolve the disagreement but _relocates_ it to how the dials are set, and that this is exactly why the book refuses a verdict: not evasion but accuracy and respect, since delivering one would merely impose an author's value weighting disguised as a conclusion.

The contested heart is now complete: inequality questioned as _function_ (Ch 18), _desert_ (Ch 19), and _justice_ (Ch 20), every position at full strength, none crowned. Part 8 widens the frame to inequality _between nations_ (Ch 21) and closes (Ch 22) with the contested "consequences of inequality" and the honest open questions the reader now carries, including the discomfort of seeing the ladder clearly without being told what to do about it.

* * *

---

Return, one last time, to Maya and Devon, the two children born the same day in the same city, whose unequal odds have followed us through the whole book. We have treated the gap between them as large, and within their society it is. But step back far enough, to the scale of the whole human species, and a startling fact comes into view: the gap between Maya and Devon, real as it is, is _smaller_ than the gap between either of them and a child born the same day in one of the world's poorest places. The single most powerful predictor of a person's life chances on this planet is not their class within their society, nor their talent, nor their effort. It is the _country they were born in_. The accident of national birth dwarfs almost every inequality we have studied, and yet it is the one we think about least, perhaps because it is the hardest to see from inside any single nation.

This chapter widens the sociological eye to its fullest aperture: inequality not up and down one society's ladder, but _between societies_ , the global stratification of the human race. It is a vast subject, and we treat it briefly and carefully, with two disciplines held especially tight. The first is the comparative eye of Chapter 1, now global: no society is the human default, and we will be fair to every society, including the reader's own and including those one might be tempted to caricature. The second is the as-of-and-direction discipline of Chapter 2: global data are harder and more uncertain than national data, so we will speak in directions and rough magnitudes, and flag what is contested, more carefully than anywhere else.


### 21.1 Two inequalities in one world

To think clearly about global inequality, you must first separate two things that combine into it, because they have moved in _opposite directions_ in recent decades, and confusing them produces nonsense.

#### Definition: Between-Country vs. Within-Country Inequality

**Between-country inequality** is the gap in average incomes _across_ nations, the difference between living in a rich country and a poor one. **Within-country inequality** is the gap between rich and poor _inside_ a single nation, the subject of the rest of this book. _Global inequality_ , the inequality among all the world's people considered together as if humanity were one society, is a combination of both: how unequal nations are from each other, plus how unequal people are within each nation.

In plain language: global inequality has two sources, the gap _between_ countries and the gap _inside_ them, and the total depends on both. For most of the last two centuries, the dominant source was _between-country_ inequality. The great divergence of the industrial era opened an enormous gap between the few countries that industrialized early and the rest, so that by the late twentieth century, where you were born mattered far more than your class within your birthplace, the bulk of global inequality was the gap between nations, not within them.

But in recent decades this has been shifting, and the shift is one of the most consequential facts of our era. As several populous countries in the global middle, China above all, and India and others, have grown rapidly, their average incomes have risen toward those of the rich world, _narrowing the between-country gap_. At the same time, within-country inequality has _risen_ in many nations, rich and developing alike. So the two components have moved oppositely: between-country inequality falling as poorer populous nations catch up, within-country inequality rising in many places. The net effect on _global_ inequality (the two combined) appears to be a modest decline, driven by the sheer demographic weight of the catching-up countries, though this is measured with real uncertainty and the trend is debated. The economist Branko Milanovic, in his 2016 book _Global Inequality_ , describes this as among the largest reshufflings of world incomes in two centuries, and whatever the precise figures, the direction is clear enough to state: the world's people, taken as a whole, have become somewhat _less_ unequal even as many individual societies have become _more_ so.

### 21.2 The elephant in the data

There is a famous way of seeing this reshuffling, a chart drawn by Branko Milanovic and Christoph Lakner that was thought to resemble an elephant, and the image captures the human story better than any single number.

Imagine lining up every person in the world from poorest to richest and asking how much each point along that line gained, in income, over a recent multi-decade stretch (roughly 1988 to 2008 in the original Lakner-Milanovic work). The resulting curve has a distinctive shape. Down in the middle of the global distribution, there is a great hump of large gains, this is the rising global middle, hundreds of millions of people in the catching-up countries (the populous parts of Asia above all) whose incomes grew dramatically, lifting unprecedented numbers out of the deepest poverty. Then, around the level corresponding to the working and lower-middle classes of the _rich_ countries, the curve sags into a trough of near-stagnation, these are the people, in the wealthy nations, whose incomes grew slowly or barely at all over the same period. And then, at the very top, the curve shoots upward again, the global top, whose gains were large. A hump, a trough, and a raised tip: a rough elephant, head down, trunk up.

The elephant is worth dwelling on because it tells, in one shape, a story of _winners and losers that crosses national lines in a way our national politics rarely captures_. The great winners include the rising middle of the developing world, an enormous and genuine human achievement, the fastest reduction in mass poverty in history. The relative losers, the trough, include the lower-middle classes of the rich countries, whose stagnation is part of the within-country inequality story of the rest of this book, and whose discontent has reshaped the politics of many wealthy nations. And the top gained handsomely everywhere. None of this is a verdict, it is a description, and like all the descriptions in this book it informs the contested questions of cause and justice without settling them. But it reframes them globally: the same decades that saw stagnation and rising inequality _within_ rich countries saw a historic _narrowing_ between countries, and whether one calls the period good or bad for "inequality" depends entirely on which inequality, and whose, one has in view.

#### Common Misconception

A common error, found across the political spectrum, is to tell the global inequality story as if it were simple and as if it pointed to an obvious verdict. One version says: "Global inequality is falling, so things are getting better, stop complaining." Another says: "Inequality is rising everywhere, the system is failing." Both are too simple, because they collapse the two components. Global _between_ -country inequality has fallen (a real and largely positive development, hundreds of millions lifted from deep poverty); _within_ -country inequality has risen in many places (the source of real and rising discontent). Both are true at once, and which you emphasize is partly a choice about which inequality matters most, a choice with a value component. Moreover, even the "falling global inequality" story carries caveats: it is measured with uncertainty, it depends heavily on the growth of a few populous countries (so it could reverse), and, as Milanovic and others note, _absolute_ gaps in income (as opposed to _ratios_) have on most cross-country measures continued to widen even as relative inequality fell, because a given percentage gain for a rich person is far more dollars than the same percentage for a poor one. The honest global picture is genuinely two-sided, and anyone who gives you a one-sided version, in either direction, is simplifying a story whose whole meaning lies in its complexity.

### 21.3 Fairness to every society

The global frame demands a discipline the national frame could let slide: fairness to _every_ society, including ones a reader may be inclined to admire or to caricature. Two examples, handled with deliberate care, show what this requires.

Consider the great growth stories of the catching-up countries, China most prominently. The reduction of mass poverty in China over recent decades is, by any honest measure, one of the most significant improvements in human welfare in history, hundreds of millions of people lifted from deep deprivation, an enormous gain in life chances at a civilizational scale. To tell the global inequality story while sneering at or minimizing this achievement, out of political distaste, would be a failure of the comparative eye and of basic fairness. _And_ , with the same even hand, China's own _within_ -country inequality rose substantially during that growth, and its arrangements carry their own contested features, so honoring the achievement does not require ignoring the complications. The discipline is to do both: state the genuine, massive gain plainly, and note the within-country inequality and contested features plainly, without letting admiration become propaganda or criticism become caricature. The same evenhandedness applies to the reader's own society, whatever it is: its achievements stated fairly, its inequalities stated plainly, no nation treated as the human default and none as the villain.

This matters beyond good manners, because the global frame is uniquely prone to a particular distortion: using _other_ societies as mirrors for one's _own_ politics, praising or damning a foreign country not on its own terms but as a stand-in for a domestic argument. The sociological eye resists this. It asks what is genuinely true of each society, in its own context, with its own history and its own as-of, and it refuses to flatten the astonishing diversity of how human societies arrange inequality into a simple ranking of good and bad nations. Every society sorts its people; each does so differently; and understanding the differences, fairly, is far more illuminating than scoring them.

### 21.4 The arbitrariness at the bottom of everything

We end this chapter where the whole book's deepest question quietly waits. The single largest determinant of a person's life chances is the country of their birth, and no one chooses the country of their birth. It is the purest case of the morally arbitrary factor that has haunted every chapter of Part 7: a circumstance entirely outside the person's control, doing more to shape their life than anything they will ever do, choose, or earn.

This observation does something uncomfortable to the arguments we have built. The whole apparatus of merit and desert and fair process, the meritocracy debate, the Rawls-Nozick clash, was developed largely _within_ the frame of a single society. But if where you are born matters more than anything you do, then the global frame presses every one of those debates to their limit. Does the difference principle apply across borders, or only within them? Is a person _entitled_ , in Nozick's sense, to the vast advantage of a rich-country birth they did nothing to acquire? Does the arbitrariness of national birth, even larger than the arbitrariness of class birth, strengthen the structural side of Thread C to its breaking point, or does the sheer impracticality of global redistribution change what justice can even require? These are real questions, and notice that the book does with them exactly what it has done throughout: it poses them in their full difficulty and declines to answer them, because they are contested OUGHTs that depend on value premises, about the scope of justice, about what we owe strangers across borders, that no fact can settle and that reasonable people answer in profoundly different ways.

We raise them here not to resolve them but because the global frame is where the book's central tension reaches its widest stretch, and because seeing it is part of seeing the ladder whole. The same eye that learned, in Chapter 1, to find the familiar strange must finally turn on the most familiar fact of all, that we draw the boundaries of our moral concern at the edges of our own society, and ask whether that boundary is a feature of justice or merely a habit of it. The book does not tell you. It only makes sure you have seen the question. In the final chapter, we gather all the threads, confront the most politically loaded claim about inequality's _effects_ , and close on the honest discomfort of a reader who can now see the whole ladder clearly and has not been told what to do about it.


### 21.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Distinguish between-country and within-country inequality, and explain how they have moved in "opposite directions" in recent decades.

Hint

One is the gap across nations; one is the gap inside nations. What did the growth of populous middle countries do to the first, and what happened to the second in many places?

**Answer:** _Between-country inequality_ is the gap in average incomes _across_ nations (the difference between living in a rich vs. a poor country); _within-country inequality_ is the gap between rich and poor _inside_ a single nation. They have moved oppositely in recent decades: _between-country_ inequality has _fallen_ as several populous middle-income countries (China above all, plus India and others) grew rapidly and their average incomes rose toward the rich world's, narrowing the gap between nations; meanwhile _within-country_ inequality has _risen_ in many nations, rich and developing alike. Global inequality (the two combined, treating humanity as one society) appears to have declined modestly, driven by the demographic weight of the catching-up countries, though measured with real uncertainty. Confusing the two components produces nonsense, because the same period was one of _falling_ inequality between countries and _rising_ inequality within many of them.

**Q2.** Describe the "elephant curve" and what each of its three features (hump, trough, raised tip) represents.

Hint

Line up all the world's people poorest to richest; plot how much each point gained over recent decades. Who is in the global middle, who is around the rich-world lower-middle, and who is at the top?

**Answer:** The elephant curve plots, for everyone in the world lined up from poorest to richest, how much income each point gained over a recent multi-decade stretch; the shape roughly resembles an elephant. The _hump_ (large gains in the global middle) represents the rising global middle, hundreds of millions in the catching-up countries (populous Asia above all) whose incomes grew dramatically, the fastest reduction in mass poverty in history. The _trough_ (near-stagnation around the level of the rich countries' working and lower-middle classes) represents people in wealthy nations whose incomes grew slowly or barely at all, part of the within-country inequality story, and a source of major political discontent. The _raised tip_ (large gains at the very top) represents the global top. The curve tells a story of _winners and losers crossing national lines_ : the developing-world middle and the global top gained, while the rich-world lower-middle stagnated, which is why the same decades look like progress or failure depending on whose inequality you have in view.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A commentator says: "Global inequality is falling, so all the worry about inequality is overblown." Another says: "Inequality is rising everywhere, the system is broken." Using the two components and the ratio-vs-absolute distinction, explain why both are too simple.

Hint

Which inequality is each talking about? Can global between-country inequality fall while within-country inequality rises? And does "relative inequality falling" mean absolute gaps are shrinking?

**Answer:** Both collapse the two components and ignore a measurement subtlety. The first commentator points to falling _global between-country_ inequality (real, largely positive, hundreds of millions lifted from deep poverty) but ignores _rising within-country_ inequality in many nations, the genuine source of much discontent, so "worry is overblown" is too simple. The second points to rising _within-country_ inequality but ignores the historic _narrowing between_ countries, so "rising everywhere" is false as stated. Both are partly true and partly false because the two components moved oppositely. Additionally, the ratio-vs-absolute distinction complicates the optimistic story: even where _relative_ (ratio) inequality fell, _absolute_ gaps in income have often continued to _widen_ , because a given percentage gain for a rich person is far more dollars than the same percentage for a poor one. So even "global inequality is falling" depends on measuring relative rather than absolute gaps. The honest picture is two-sided and measured with uncertainty, and which side one emphasizes carries a value component (which inequality matters most); anyone giving a one-sided version is simplifying a story whose meaning lies in its complexity.

**Q2.** The chapter insists on stating China's poverty reduction as "one of the most significant improvements in human welfare in history" _and_ noting its rising within-country inequality, without letting "admiration become propaganda or criticism become caricature." Explain why the global frame is especially prone to the distortion of "using other societies as mirrors for one's own politics," and what the comparative eye requires instead.

Hint

When people praise or damn a foreign country, are they always judging it on its own terms? What does fairness to every society (including one's own) require?

**Answer:** The global frame is especially prone to this distortion because foreign societies are easy to use as _stand-ins for domestic arguments_ : a person may praise or damn another country not on its own terms but to score a point in their own society's politics (holding it up as a model to emulate or a warning to avoid), which distorts the actual facts of that society. The comparative eye requires instead asking what is _genuinely true of each society, in its own context, with its own history and as-of_ , and refusing to flatten the diversity of how societies arrange inequality into a simple ranking of good and bad nations. Concretely, for China it requires stating _both_ the genuine, massive welfare gain (hundreds of millions lifted from deep poverty) _and_ the rising within-country inequality and contested features, plainly and evenly, letting neither admiration become propaganda nor criticism become caricature. The same evenhandedness applies to the reader's _own_ society (achievements stated fairly, inequalities plainly) and forbids treating any nation as the human default or the villain. Fairness to every society is not mere politeness; it is the condition of seeing global inequality accurately rather than through the lens of one's domestic loyalties.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** The chapter observes that the country of one's birth, which no one chooses, is the single largest determinant of life chances, an even larger "morally arbitrary factor" than class. Apply the Rawls-Nozick debate of Chapter 20 to the _global_ scale. Does the arbitrariness of national birth strengthen the case for global redistribution, and what are the strongest objections? Why does the book pose this without answering it?

**Discussion:** This question stretches the book's central tension to its widest, and it shows both the power and the limits of carrying the national justice debate across borders.

The case that national arbitrariness strengthens global redistributive duties (a Rawls-extended view): Rawls's deepest move was that morally arbitrary factors, things you did nothing to deserve, have no claim to determine your life prospects, and that justice requires arranging inequalities to benefit the worst-off. If the _class_ you are born into is morally arbitrary, the _country_ you are born into is even more so, and it matters even more for your life chances. So, the argument runs, consistency demands extending the concern: if we owe the worst-off in our own society an arrangement that benefits them, why not the worst-off in the world, whose disadvantage flows from an even more arbitrary accident? Behind a _global_ veil of ignorance, not knowing which country you would be born into, you would surely choose principles protecting against being born into deep poverty. On this view, the arbitrariness of national birth presses powerfully toward duties that cross borders.

The strongest objections come from several directions. A _Nozickian_ objection: even granting national birth is arbitrary, it does not follow that anyone is _entitled_ to take the holdings of the rich-country-born to redistribute globally; entitlement depends on how holdings arose, not on the arbitrariness of who holds them, and arbitrariness of starting point does not by itself license confiscation. A _scope-of-justice_ objection (held by many who are otherwise sympathetic to Rawls): principles of distributive justice may apply _within_ a shared political community, with its shared institutions and mutual obligations, and may simply not extend, or extend only weakly, to strangers with whom one shares no such community, so global duties might be real but of a different and lesser kind (humanitarian rather than distributive-justice duties). A _practical_ objection: even if the duty existed, there is no global institution capable of just redistribution, and attempts might do more harm than good, so what justice can _require_ is constrained by what is feasible. And a _self-determination_ objection: peoples have a legitimate interest in governing their own societies, and a country's prosperity may partly reflect its own institutional choices, complicating the claim that rich-country advantage is purely arbitrary windfall.

Why does the book pose this without answering it? For exactly the reason it has declined every verdict: the question turns on contested value premises that no fact can settle, here, the _scope_ of justice (does it stop at borders?), what we _owe strangers_ versus fellow citizens, how _entitlement_ relates to arbitrariness, and how much _feasibility_ constrains obligation. Reasonable, informed, good-faith people answer these profoundly differently, and a book that delivered a verdict would simply be imposing one contestable answer about the scope of moral concern and calling it knowledge. What the book _can_ do is show you that the morally arbitrary factor it has tracked all along, unchosen circumstance shaping life chances, reaches its largest form at the global scale, and that this presses the justice debate to its limit. Whether the boundary of your moral concern at your society's edge is a _feature_ of justice or merely a _habit_ of it is, like every deep question in this book, yours to decide, now that you have seen it clearly, which, here as everywhere, is the book's only goal.

### Chapter Summary

We widened the sociological eye to its fullest aperture, inequality _between nations_ , and met the startling fact that the single largest predictor of a person's life chances is the _country of their birth_ , an unchosen circumstance dwarfing the class inequalities the book has studied. We separated **between-country inequality** (the gap across nations) from **within-country inequality** (the gap inside them), which combine into _global inequality_ , and saw they have moved _oppositely_ in recent decades: between-country inequality _falling_ as populous middle countries (China above all, plus India and others) caught up, within-country inequality _rising_ in many places, with global inequality modestly declining overall (measured with real uncertainty), the greatest reshuffling of world incomes since the Industrial Revolution.

The **elephant curve** captured this in one shape: a _hump_ of large gains for the rising global middle (the fastest mass-poverty reduction in history), a _trough_ of stagnation for the rich countries' lower-middle classes (fueling their politics), and a _raised tip_ of large gains at the global top. We warned against one-sided readings in either direction (collapsing the two components), and noted that even "falling global inequality" depends on measuring _relative_ rather than _absolute_ gaps, which have often kept widening.

We held two disciplines especially tight: the _as-of-and-direction_ caution (global data are uncertain; speak in directions), and _fairness to every society_ (state China's genuine, massive welfare gain plainly _and_ its rising within-country inequality plainly, letting neither admiration become propaganda nor criticism become caricature, and applying the same evenhandedness to the reader's own society), resisting the global frame's special temptation to use foreign societies as mirrors for domestic politics.

Finally we saw that national birth is the _purest morally arbitrary factor_ of all, pressing the Part 7 justice debates (Rawls, Nozick, the scope of justice, what we owe strangers) to their widest stretch, and the book did what it always does: posed the question in full difficulty and declined to answer it, because it rests on contested value premises no fact can settle. Chapter 22 now gathers all three threads, confronts the most politically loaded claim about inequality's _consequences_ , and closes on the honest discomfort of seeing the whole ladder clearly without being told what to do about it.

* * *

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 22: What Inequality Does, and the Questions You Now Carry
blocks.src: We have come a long way from the two newborns of Chapter 1. We have measured the ladder, defined it, watched it shape lives and pass itself down, counted its bottom, read its gaps, and judged it from every serious angle. One large question about inequality remains, and it is the one most likely to ambush an unprepared thinker, because it wears the costume of settled fact while smuggling a verdict: the question of what inequality _does_ , its consequences. And then, having handled that with the discipline the whole book has built toward, we will gather our three threads, take a last look at Maya and Devon, and close, not with an answer, but with the honest discomfort of a reader who can now see the whole ladder clearly and has not been told what to do about it. That discomfort, this book will argue, is not a failure of the book. It is the book's final and most important gift.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 22: What Inequality Does, and the Questions You Now Carry
blocks.src:
### 22.1 The consequences literature, and why it is the prime site of verdict-by-disguise

There is a large and influential body of work arguing that inequality itself, not just poverty, but the _gap_ between rich and poor, causes a wide range of social harms: that more unequal societies suffer more violence, more mental illness, worse physical health, less social trust, weaker democracy, even slower or less stable economic growth. The most famous statement of this thesis, Richard Wilkinson and Kate Pickett's _The Spirit Level_ (2009), assembled cross-national correlations showing that more unequal rich countries tend to score worse on a striking array of social and health problems, and proposed a mechanism: that inequality generates status anxiety, stress, and a corrosion of the social bonds that hold a society together, harming even the well-off.

If this thesis is correct, it would seem to settle the whole argument of this book in one stroke: inequality would be not merely contestable but _demonstrably harmful_ , bad for everyone, and the verdict the book has refused to deliver would deliver itself. And that is exactly why this is the most dangerous terrain in the entire subject, and why we apply, here, the hardest version of the discipline of Chapter 12. Because the consequences literature is the _prime site of verdict-by-disguise_ : the place where a contested causal hypothesis, dressed in the authority of measured correlations, is most often presented as a settled finding that quietly establishes "inequality is bad," skipping every one of the careful steps this book has insisted on.

Apply the discipline. _Is_ there a correlation between inequality and various social problems across societies? Often, yes, that is the measured part, the IS. Does the correlation establish that inequality _causes_ those problems? No, and every caution from the Great Gatsby chapter applies with full force, and more. Correlation is not causation: more unequal societies differ from more equal ones in many ways besides their inequality (history, size, social composition, institutions, culture), any of which could drive the social outcomes. Reverse and common causes lurk: the same factors that produce social problems might produce inequality, or some third thing might produce both. And there is a subtle statistical trap specific to this literature, a version of which critics have pressed hard (arguing the correlations are sensitive to country selection and to the choice of measures): because the benefit of an additional dollar is larger for a poor person than a rich one, a society's _average_ outcome on something like health can correlate with its _inequality_ as a near-arithmetic artifact, without inequality _as such_ causing anything, the aggregate correlation can be partly an illusion arising from how individual-level relationships add up. On top of all this, the data have been contested, with critics arguing that the choice of which countries and which problems to include shapes the result, and that the relationships are weaker or vanish under different specifications.
